bio.en: Nan Yu is a product leader at Linear known for the team's belief that there is no trade-off between speed and quality when people are truly competent.
bio.zh: 南宇（Nan Yu）是 Linear 的产品负责人，以团队"在真正有能力的状态下，速度与质量之间并无折中"的信念而闻名。

summary.en: Nan argues speed and quality are not a trade-off - top crafters' output quality is visible in how fast they move. He describes having a working hypothesis tested internally within the first ~10% of a project's time. The episode covers how Linear says no to features to avoid bloat and keep ICs happy.
summary.zh: 南认为速度与质量并非折中关系——顶尖匠人的产出质量，正体现在他们推进的速度上。他描述了一个做法：在项目前约 10% 的时间内，就拿出可工作的版本、在内部验证关键假设。本期涵盖了 Linear 如何通过拒绝功能来避免臃肿、让一线工程师满意。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think you see in the team at Linear that a lot of people don't see, which is that there's not actually a trade-off between speed and quality.
turns.zh: 我觉得在Linear团队里，你们看到了许多人没能意识到的一点，那就是速度和质量之间其实并不存在权衡取舍。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: People talk about this as if there were a trade-off because when they think about speed, the thing they over-index on is rushing or being sloppy. What they should be indexing on is being really competent. If you look at people who are at the pinnacle of their craft, you can basically tell how good the output is going to be of their work product by how fast they're going.
turns.zh: 人们谈论这个问题时，总把它当作一种权衡，但其实他们在考虑速度时，往往过度关注于仓促行事或粗制滥造。真正该关注的，应该是高超的专业能力。看看那些行业顶尖高手，你基本上就能通过他们的工作效率判断出他们的成果质量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What does speed look like when you say it can be done quickly and high quality?
turns.zh: 当你说速度能做到又快又高质量时，具体表现是什么样的呢？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: What it really looks like is you have some rough time budget for how long you think something's going to take. By the time 10% of it has passed, after week one, you have something that works that tests some kind of key hypothesis internally.
turns.zh: 实际情况是，你先为某项工作设定一个大致的时间预算。比如第一周结束时，当项目完成10%时，就能产出一个可行的版本，用来验证内部的某个关键假设。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine a criticism you all get. Over time, you'll probably become a bloated piece of software as well.
turns.zh: 我想你们肯定会遇到一个批评意见：久而久之，你们也会开发出一个臃肿的软件系统。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: When we examine this problem, we look at, "Well, what feature requests can we debate and what kind of feature requests do we absolutely have to say no to?" The stuff that we absolutely have to say no to is the exact kind of thing that leads to this bloatedness that makes ICs hate their lives.
turns.zh: 当我们审视这个问题时，我们会问：“哪些功能需求可以讨论，哪些又必须拒绝？”那些必须拒绝的需求，正是导致系统臃肿、让内部客户痛不欲生的根源。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something that your head of sales shared with me is how impressed he is with the way you ask questions on customer calls and just keep digging and digging until you get to something.
turns.zh: 你们的销售主管跟我分享过，他对你们在客户电话中提问时善于深度挖掘的能力印象深刻。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: My goal is to feel bad in the same way that customers feel bad.
turns.zh: 我的目标是，能像客户一样感受到那种糟糕的体验。

turns.en: Thanks for having me. I'm a long-time listener and reader, so it's really a treat to be here.

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to share something with you to kick off that I haven't shared with you yet, that I haven't shared with anyone. turns.zh: 我想先和大家分享一个尚未公开的信息，这个调查结果可能等本期播客发布时才会公布。但我现在正在进行一项名为"你的工具堆栈里有什么？"的调查，向所有订阅者提问："你日常使用最多的工具是什么？最喜欢的工具是什么？最讨厌的工具是什么？"其中一个问题是，如果IT部门允许，你最想换成哪个工具？目前得票最多的是希望从Jira换成Linear。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Wow. I mean, hopefully, that means we're doing a good job.
turns.zh: 哇。这意味着我们做得不错吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think that's exactly what that means. I'll read a couple quotes to give you a sense of what people are saying about Linear. I doubt these are surprising to you, but this gives people a sense of why you're here and why I'm excited to extract as much wisdom as I can from you. So, a couple quotes here. "Linear is a joy to use as I interact with my engineering teams, and I find inspiration in its design." "Linear is simple to use, yet powerful." "Linear's design is obviously an industry benchmark, but moreover, the performance and speed is a massive productivity boost."
turns.zh: 我觉得这正是这个结果的意义所在。我会读几条用户对Linear的评价，让大家感受一下他们对Linear的看法。我相信这些评价对你们来说并不意外，但能让大家明白你们为何会来到这里，以及我为何迫切希望能从你们这里汲取尽可能多的智慧。接下来是几条评价："在与工程团队互动时，Linear用起来非常顺手，我从它的设计中获得了灵感。" "Linear简单易用，却功能强大。" "Linear的设计显然是行业标杆，但更重要的是，它的性能和速度极大提升了生产力"

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: I mean, it's really good to hear that because in a lot of ways, that's what we're trying to do. If you think about the entire impetus behind why Linear was started, it's because Karri was sitting at Coinbase and Airbnb and these places and just watching everyone around him struggle using the tools that they had available and always incumbent tools and just seeing that it made people hate their day-to-day a little bit, and we all got into technology and design and engineering, all this kind of stuff because it was fun. All of us started off building stupid MySpace pages and all of these side projects when we were young, and it started off as this fun thing that we do, and we're like, "Wow, we get to do this for a career," and then to have all of this kind of stuff put these big speed bumps into our day-to-day workflow, it just was really sad. So, that's why we started Linear. This really bust through all of that.
turns.zh: 听到这些评价真是太好了。因为在很多方面，这正是我们努力的方向。回想起创立Linear的初衷，源于Karri在Coinbase和Airbnb等公司工作，目睹身边的人使用现有工具（往往是传统的专有工具）时举步维艰，工作效率低下。这让我们深有感触——毕竟，我们当初投身技术、设计和工程领域，正是因为热爱这些领域，享受其中的乐趣。年轻时，我们曾建过傻傻的MySpace页面，搞过各种副业项目，最终将兴趣发展成职业，却不料工作流程被各种障碍阻塞，这实在令人沮丧。所以我们创立了Linear，彻底打破了这些障碍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I love about Linear, I feel like it's an inspirational business because many people want to, "I'm going to build just a much better version of something," and often that doesn't actually work out. Often nobody cares enough. There's all these barriers and reasons. People don't switch to something that's better, and Linear is an amazing example of building an excellent product and actually succeeding, and there's a lot more to it maybe than just building an awesome product. So, that's what I'm excited to dig into and understand how you all operate, and I guess just based on these results, to me, this is the ultimate sign of product market fit. People being sad they can't use a product in B2B enterprise software especially, so let's get into it. (00:07:52): First question I want to get into is something that I think you see and the team at Linear sees that a lot of people don't see, which is that there's not actually a trade-off between speed and quality. I think a lot of people think this is just an innate fact and something I've heard you talk about is that's not actually true. I actually saw Patrick Collison tweet this exact point that I'll read after you... I want to hear your thoughts, but talk about what you've learned about how there's maybe not actually this trade-off between speed and quality.
turns.zh: 关于 Linear 让我最为着迷的地方在于，它是一家极具启发性的企业。许多人总想说：“我要打造一款比现有产品更出色的版本”，但往往事与愿违。往往没人足够上心。存在着种种障碍和阻力——用户不愿迁移到更优质的产品。Linear 却成功打造了卓越的产品并获得了巨大成功，其秘诀或许不止于产品本身。因此，我迫切想深入了解你们的运营之道。我认为从这些成果来看，这正是产品与市场完美契合的最终证明。特别是在 B2B 企业软件领域，用户对无法使用某款产品的失落感尤为明显。接下来让我们深入探讨。（00:07:52）首先我想探讨一个我和 Linear 团队都注意到、但多数人未曾察觉的现象——速度与质量之间其实不存在权衡取舍。我知道很多人认为这是一个固有的事实，但 Patrick Collison 曾明确指出这并非事实。我读到过 Patrick 的推文，等你们分享完观点后，我想听听你们的见解。谈谈你们如何认识到速度与质量之间或许并不存在权衡。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: People talk about this as if there were a trade-off almost in a naive way because when they think about speed, the thing they over index on is rushing or being sloppy, and what they should be indexing on is being really competent or being like an expert. So, if you look at people who are at the pinnacle of their craft, it could be anything. It could be like a chef or a programmer or someone building houses or something. You can basically tell how good the output is going to be of their work product by how fast they're going. If they're going really fast, and they're obviously not being sloppy and then leaving a mess all over the place, it's like, "Yeah. Well, they got there because this is just second nature to them," and they're able to go at a really rapid pace and try stuff. And when we're building software, that's such a big component of how good the product is on the other side of it, which is like, "How many iterations were you able to do?" So, the only way you're going to get a bunch of iterations done and try different things and really feel out these different variations is by just going very fast.
turns.zh: 人们谈论这个问题时，往往以一种天真幼稚的方式认为存在权衡，因为当他们想到速度时，首先想到的是匆忙行事或粗制滥造，而他们真正应该关注的是专业能力或专家级水准。以顶尖技艺为业的人为例——无论是厨师、程序员、房屋建筑工人等——你都能通过他们的工作速度判断其产出的质量。如果他们速度极快，且显然不存在马虎行事、留下烂摊子的情况，那就说明他们对此轻车熟路，因为这已然是他们的第二天性。他们能够以极快的速度尝试新事物。当我们开发软件时，快速迭代的次数正是衡量产品质量的重要指标——即你完成了多少次迭代并尝试了不同方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: In terms of speed, is the speed there moving quickly on each of iterations? Like what does speed look like when you say, "It can be done quickly and high quality"? What does speed look like?
turns.zh: 关于速度，你们在每次迭代中是否能快速推进？当你说“既能快速完成又保证高质量”时，速度具体呈现为何种状态？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Speed... What it really looks like is you have some rough time budget for how long you think something's going to take, and by the time 10% of it has passed, you have a workable solution. It's not like, "Oh, at the halfway point, we have something that is maybe a candidate that we can play around with." It's like, no, no, no. After week one you have something that works that tests some kind of key hypothesis internally so that you can feel like is this thing actually panning out the way we expect it to or did we have some crazy incorrect assumption? And you don't want to wait until you're 80% done to be able to make that kind of judgment because then it's just too late. Then you're pushing deadlines out, and you're making your marketing team very sad.
turns.zh: 速度……其实表现为你为某项任务设定一个粗略的时间预算。当完成 10% 的任务时，你就能获得一个可行的解决方案。这不是在中途说“哦，做到一半时我们有了个可以试试的版本”。不，不，不。一周结束时，你就能得到一个可用的产品，用于验证某个关键假设，这样你就能判断产品是否正如预期发展，或者是否存在某个荒谬的错误假设。你不想等到完成 80% 后才做出判断，因为那时已经太晚了。你只会不断推迟截止日期，让营销团队倍感失望。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay, so the way you think is, "We're going to spend a month on this feature. Let's get something workable. We can start testing with potential users even internally in the first few days, essentially in the first week"?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，你的思路是：“我们要花一个月时间开发这个功能。先做个能用的版本。前几天甚至第一周就能在内部测试潜在用户了。”

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yes. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I guess how can you do that? Because most teams can't do that. Most teams need to research, design, build. "Okay, cool. We have something," and once a month later, what allows you to do that?
turns.zh: 对啊。我想知道你们是怎么做到的？因为大多数团队做不到这一点。大多数团队需要先调研、设计、开发。然后说：“好吧，不错。我们有成果了”，可一个月后再回头看，你们是怎么做到的？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, there's a lot of components of it. I think having really good talent really helps. Having engineers who don't get blocked by every single little design choice, they're happy to just make something workable. Even if they don't feel comfortable with that particular solution, they'll just bust through it and make something happen there. Part of it is intent. We don't have any expectation that the first version of it is going to be great. That is not in the cards. Look, the first version of it is our best guess in the general direction of what we want to actually ship in the end, and sometimes it works out. Sometimes, it's like, "Wow, this first version was pretty good. Let's make some minor adjustments, and we're good to go," but there's no expectation there. So, no one feels like they have to be a perfectionist and get everything, like all sanded down and really in tip-top shape. It just has to work and get the job done and validate or invalidate our major assumptions.
turns.zh: 是的，这里面有很多因素。我觉得拥有优秀的人才非常重要。工程师们不会被每个小设计决策困住，他们乐于先做个能用的版本。即便对某个特定解决方案不满意，他们也会突破难关，完成任务。关键在于初衷。我们不期望第一个版本就完美无缺。这根本不现实。记住，第一个版本只是我们对最终发布产品大方向的最佳猜测，有时成功，有时则需要调整优化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'll read this quote from Patrick Collison. He tweeted this today as I was preparing for this interview, and he's the CEO and founder of Stripe, if you're not familiar. His tweet is, "I increasingly believe that 'good, cheap, fast -- choose two' maxim is devious misinformation spread by the slow. In my experience, slow and expensive usually go together."
turns.zh: 我要引用帕特里克·科里森（Patrick Collison）的一句话。他今天发了这条推文，正好我准备这次采访时看到了。他是Stripe的CEO和创始人，如果你不熟悉的话。他写道：“我越来越相信‘好、便宜、快——选两个’这种说法是慢悠悠的人散布的诡计。以我的经验，慢和贵往往如影随形。”

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. I mean, use the contractor kind of example. Like If someone's making modifications to their house, and it's taking forever, one, you're in a hotel and also the bills are adding up.
turns.zh: 是啊，就是这样。比如用承包商做例子。比如有人改造房子，拖拖拉拉，一来，你住在酒店，费用不断增加。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The other example you used when we were chatting about this earlier is chess players. I'm thinking of Magnus Carlsen, watching him. I think he was number one in speed chess in addition to just regular chess and what a microcosm of this point.
turns.zh: 你之前和我们聊这个时提到的另一个例子是国际象棋选手。我想到马格努斯·卡尔森（Magnus Carlsen），除了常规比赛，他还是速度象棋冠军，简直是这观点的缩影。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, I think that's the case and Magnus and Hikaru and all those guys who are at the top of their game, they can go unbelievably fast. In fact, that's the usual... I mean, I don't want to get too out of my depth with chess, but the usual way you try to make the game fair is you give them much, much less time than someone who's not quite as strong of a player, and they'll still win a lot of time, too.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得确实如此。马格努斯、木村光希（Hikaru Nakamura）这些顶级选手，他们速度快得惊人。事实上，通常……我不想在象棋上深究，但常见的让比赛公平的方式是给他们比弱棋手少得多的时间，他们照样能赢得大量时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, maybe just to close out this point and give someone something concrete they can do with this information, say they want to start moving faster while not cutting quality, what do you think they can do? What's one thing they can start trying to work on and improving in the way they operate?
turns.zh: 那么，或许总结一下这个观点，让大家能具体应用这些信息。比如他们想在不牺牲质量的前提下提高速度，你觉得他们能做什么？在操作方式上可以从哪方面改进？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: I think it's really that sort of attitude and point of view question to understand and take the almost controlled risk that the first version of this is not going to be perfect. So, it actually makes it a lot cheaper in many ways. It means you don't need a pixel perfect design. It means you don't need to make sure that all of the little UI bugs and stuff like that are solved because none of that really matters. What matters is you have working software that you can interact with, and you can see if it feels good. Does it actually solve the core problem that is facing our users? You can take it back to users. You can even let them into an early beta or something like that and get real validation there and to really focus on getting the smallest, shippable element, like not shippable in the sense of, "I can actually put on the production," but in the sense of like, "I can start learning from here."
turns.zh: 我认为关键在于，要有这样的态度和思维方式：理解并接受初版产品可能存在的不完美，接受近乎可控的风险。从很多方面来说，这反而能降低成本。例如，你无需追求像素级完美的设计，也不必确保所有微小的UI漏洞都被解决——这些都无关紧要。重要的是，你要拥有可供用户交互的实用软件，验证其是否符合用户需求。是否能真正解决用户面临的核心问题？你可以将产品交付给用户，甚至让他们参与早期测试，从中获取真实反馈，专注于提取最小的、可交付的功能模块——这里的“可交付”并非指“可以上线生产”，而是指“可以从中汲取经验”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just a question I imagine is in everyone's mind is what do you do with this first very ugly V1... not ugly, not fully ready, first version. Is this something you're using internally to see if it's something? Is it something you have beta design partners with?
turns.zh: 我猜大家都好奇：如何处理这款初版V1？它丑陋又不成熟，功能不完善。你们内部会测试吗？有没有Beta版合作伙伴？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: We have a gradually increasing sort of circle of users that use every single feature. So, by the time it hits GA, by the time it gets released, it's been used by a lot of different users up to that point. So, the first circle is just internal users. We use Linear every single day to write software and do our own work, so we have that kind of advantage and then once we feel like it's good enough, we'll put it into some beta customer group, and again, as early as we can in the process. We have to make sure that we don't end up corrupting people's data, and it doesn't look hideous and that kind of stuff, but as long as it reaches that level of quality, we can release it to early access customers who can give us good feedback and also just try to solve their problems with it. If no one engages with it, if no one's using it, then that's a good signal that we didn't really hit the mark, and then we have a couple of different beta audiences that we grow and then the ultimate release obviously is for GA where everyone gets it.
turns.zh: 我们会逐步扩大用户群体，确保每个功能都经过实战检验。GA版本（正式发布）前，绝大多数用户都已使用过相关功能。最初仅限内部用户使用，我们日常开发都依赖Linear，因此拥有天然优势。达到足够成熟度后，我们会尽早开放Beta测试，并持续收集反馈。关键是避免数据损坏，避免界面过于丑陋。只要达到基本质量标准，就能推送给早期用户，让他们提供反馈并解决实际问题。若无人使用，说明方向错误——这时我们会调整测试群体，最终正式发布。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an amazing answer. Okay, so secret number one to Linear success, I'm going to take some notes here, is get new feature, product ideas out to people as early as possible, say, in the first 10% of the amount of time you've allotted, and then release it increasingly to more and more people to get feedback. I think the implication here is just most wasted time is on building things nobody actually ends up wanting or using. So, the sooner you at least get directional sense of are you heading in a good direction, the faster it all go?
turns.zh: 太棒了。第一条Lean成败秘诀是：尽早让用户试用新功能，占用不超过10%的开发周期。然后逐步扩大测试范围，快速收集反馈。这意味着避免在没人需要的产品上浪费时间。早期获得方向指引，能让进程更高效吧？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, totally.
turns.zh: 完全赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine a criticism you all get. People are like, "Yes, Linear is so great, so beautiful, so much better than what's been out there for decades," but over time you'll probably become a bloated piece of software as well. That's just the fate of enterprise software. You have to check all these checkboxes. IT teams need all these features. So, there's always this like, "Oh, yeah, sure, you guys can operate this way for now. You have an amazing product for now, but it'll get ugly and bloated." How do you think about avoiding that? I know it's something you spent a lot of time thinking about. Maybe give us a glimpse into some of the conversations you have internally when there's these feature requests like, "Oh, I need single sign-on with this thing and this button here." How do you think about what to add, what not to add, and how to add these features to not make it bloated?
turns.zh: 我能想象到你们常遇到的批评。人们会说：“没错，Linear 确实很棒，界面美观，远超市面上几十年来那些老旧的产品。”但随着时间推移，你们很可能也会变成一款臃肿的软件。这就是企业级软件的宿命——必须满足各种条条框框，IT团队总会要求一堆功能。所以总会有人说：“哦，是啊，现在你们还能这么操作。你们的产品确实很棒，但迟早会变得又丑又臃肿。” 你们如何避免这种情况？我知道这确实是你们花了大量心思去思考的问题。或许能跟我们透露一下内部的讨论过程？比如当收到诸如“我需要与这个系统实现单点登录，点击这里那个按钮”之类的功能需求时，团队是如何权衡取舍的？如何在添加新功能时避免让产品变得复杂又笨重？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: This question actually comes to us a lot from candidates that are interviewing with us. When you go like, "Hey, do you have any questions for us?" This is the question that we're going to get. So, we hear it quite a lot, and it's very sensible for them to ask it because they see history being littered with the corpses of startups trying to compete in this space and not making it, and I think when we examine this problem, we look at, "Well, what kind of feature requests can we debate and what kind of feature requests do we absolutely have to say no to?" And the stuff that we absolutely have to say no to is also the exact kind of thing that leads to this bloatedness that makes ICs hate their lives, and it's very specific. It's customization features requested by middle managers in order to make reporting a little bit easier at the cost of making IC workflows worse. (00:17:16): It's like if it fits that description, we're just saying, "No." There's no debate because we've already thought about it and this is the thing that we can't take a single step down this path. So, I think that's honestly one of the core promises of Linear is that we will not make this particular trade-off. So, when you see people saying like, "Wow, Linear is so much faster. It's so much easier to use and it makes my work so much more enjoyable." This is the reason because we have not taken a single step in this direction. It's very easy for a PM to say yes to this kind of request because often they're talking with buyers. Any kind of B2B type of space, they're talking with whoever the gatekeeper is and sales is putting pressure on them, and they're saying like, "Hey, we really want this one feature. It's going to make our reporting nicer." (00:18:02): So, the director's going to be really excited by this, and we'll definitely make a buying decision based off of this, and we have to convince them that this is a false trade-off. The whole premise is wrong because the moment you start going down this path, and you make the IC user experience worse, they're just going to disengage. No one has to do this. If I'm an engineer, I get paid to write code. My performance review is based on my code contribution. It's not based on like, "Did I fill in all the tickets right?" So, I'm just not going to do that part, or I'm going to do it very sporadically, and then I'm going to just focus on my actual job. (00:18:38): And then all your reporting is wrong because all the data is wrong, and it's sparse, and you get situations where people will... They'll say like, "Well, here's a dropdown field that someone put in here that's required." There's nine choices. I don't know what any of them meet, so I'm just going to pick one at random. I'm still going to pick the first one. Also, I'm going to pray that my boss is not actually using this data to do any kind of reporting and that has consequence because the data can't possibly be correct. So, I think for us, it's a very easy decision when it comes to that particular category of feature request.
turns.zh:
事实上，我们经常从面试我们的候选人那里听到这个问题。当他们问“嘿，你们有什么问题想问我们吗？”时，我们就会收到这个问题。我们经常听到这个问题，而且候选人这样问是明智的，因为他们看到历史上许多初创公司试图在这一领域竞争却失败了，所以我们需要审视这个问题：哪些功能需求可以讨论，哪些又必须拒绝？而那些必须拒绝的功能，往往正是导致IC们痛苦不堪的根源。

（00:17:16）：只要符合这个描述，我们就会直接说“不行”。无需讨论，因为我们已经深思熟虑过，这个方向我们绝不会走。所以我认为，这正是Linear的核心承诺之一——我们绝不会做出这种权衡取舍。这就是为什么人们会说：“哇，Linear速度快多了，用起来轻松多了，工作也愉快多了。”这就是原因，因为我们从不走这条路。产品经理很容易对这类需求说“行”——毕竟他们常与采购方沟通。在B2B领域，他们面对的是决策者和销售的施压：“我们特别需要这个功能，它能优化报告体验。”

（00:18:02）：但总监们往往会为此兴奋不已，认为这就是购买决策的依据。但我们必须让他们相信这是一个错误的权衡。整个前提就是错的，因为一旦走上这条路，就会损害IC的用户体验，他们就会逐渐失去兴趣。没人需要这样做。作为工程师，我的工作就是写代码，绩效评估基于代码贡献量，而不是“我是否正确填写了所有工单”。所以我不会参与这部分工作，或者只是偶尔应付了事，然后专注于本职工作。

（00:18:38）：最终所有报告数据都会出错、稀缺化。人们会说：“某人添加了一个必填的下拉菜单，有九个选项，我根本不知道哪个合适，我就随便选一个。”然后祈祷老板不会用这些数据做报告，因为数据根本不准确。所以对我们来说，面对这类功能需求，决策非常简单：优先考虑IC，忽视中层管理者。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how simple and clear that is. Basically, you all have a policy. We'll prioritize ICs over middle managers. Especially, like I love that it's around reporting. Almost always it sounds like, "I want to track what's happening."
turns.zh: 这真是简单明了。基本上，贵公司有明确的政策——优先考虑IC，忽视中层管理者。特别是关于报告的部分，我特别赞同。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. It's always, "I want to track what's happening." Well, what do you want to track? Well, I want to track which version of the product this thing's tied to based on some field information. It's like, okay, how is the person working on this supposed to even know that information? Well, it takes like a five-minute scavenger hunt every single time. It's like, "I don't think they're going to do that, man."
turns.zh: 是啊，没错。人们总是说：“我要追踪正在发生什么事。”好吧，那你想追踪什么？嗯，我想根据某些字段信息，追踪这个产品与哪个版本相关。问题是，负责这项工作的人怎么能知道这些信息呢？每次都要花五分钟到处找资料。人们会说：“我觉得他们不会这么做的。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I imagine happens, and I think why this is hard for most companies is there's an implication that you're turning down deals. You're not adding that one feature that will close a massive million-dollar sale, very difficult to do. I imagine it helps a lot that... I imagine the COO is very bought into this and there's this, "We will win long-term holding the line on this." Is that right?
turns.zh: 我能想象的情况是，我觉得大多数公司之所以觉得这很难，是因为这暗示着你会拒绝一些交易。你不去添加那个能促成百万美元大单的功能，这太难做到了。我觉得关键在于……我觉得首席运营官对此非常认同，他们会说：“我们会长期坚持这一点，坚持到底。”对吧？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: So, it is, but I also think that there's not as much pressure as you would expect to do these kinds of things. There are basic scaling things, like we had to make SAML and SCIM and that kind of stuff. It's like, "Yeah, sure, we're going to do those sorts of, like keep the lights on type of work," but when it comes to work that's related to the actual business logic of the app's value proposition, what buyers care about is, is this going to make their team more effective? That's the reason that they're making this buying decision in the first place is that they're like, "Well, the current situation we're in... " And especially with large companies, right? The current situation we're in is a mess, and if we can convince them that these types of things are actually the reason that it's a mess, then we can really navigate them out of wanting them in the first place.
turns.zh: 所以，确实如此，但我觉得做这类事情的压力并没有你想象的那么大。比如，基本的扩展工作，比如我们必须实现SAML和SCIM之类的东西。人们会说：“好吧，没问题，我们会做这些维持基本运转的工作，”但当涉及到与应用程序价值主张的实际业务逻辑相关的工作，买家关心的是，这能让他们的团队更高效吗？他们做出购买决策的初衷就是因为他们会说：“好吧，我们目前的处境……” 尤其是对大公司来说，对吧？他们目前的处境一团糟，如果我们能让他们相信这些问题的原因在于缺乏这些功能，那我们就能真正引导他们意识到，正是这些功能让他们的处境变得一团糟。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So, there's an element of you think you need this, but it turns out you'll be more successful and get everything you want, not getting this?
turns.zh: 明白了。所以，有种情况是你觉得自己需要这个功能，但结果发现不做反而更成功，能得到你想要的一切？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, and the thing is, it's not everything you want, right? Because people come with a laundry list, and it's like laundry list. Here's 10 things I want. You're like, "Do you want all of those 10 things equally?" They're like, "No, actually I don't." The first three are the things that really matter to us. If we solve the first three, then the other stuff, we can negotiate on. So, our job is to solve the first three-way better than anybody else that if they got through the first three through some kind of visual programming, customization type of thing, that it's never going to get to the quality level and the depth that we're able to offer by offering those as native features.
turns.zh: 是啊，但问题是，并非他们想要的一切都同样重要，对吧？因为人们会列出一长串需求，但这不过是清单而已。比如，这里有10个我想要的东西。你会问：“你对这10个东西的需求程度都一样吗？”他们会说：“不，其实不一样。”前三个才是对我们真正重要的。如果我们能解决前三个问题，那么其他部分我们可以协商解决。所以，我们的任务是比其他任何人更好地解决前三个问题。如果他们通过某种可视化编程、定制之类的手段解决了前三个问题，那最终的质量和深度永远达不到我们通过原生功能提供的水平。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting thinking back to that survey I shared where the tool people want to switch to if IT allowed them was Linear, and on the one hand you could argue, "Well, okay, IT is not letting them use Linear for all these reasons. On the other hand, you guys are growing really quickly within enterprise, like you're a new business. You started, I think, mid-market startups, and now you're working way up. So, I think it's not fair to say it's not going to work in enterprise. It's clearly working really well. I don't know if there's any stats you can share anything of that, but it seems to be going well, expanding up market.
turns.zh: 回想起我分享的那项调查很有意思，IT部门如果允许的话，他们想换用的工具是Linear。一方面，你可以说：“好吧，那IT部门不让他们用Linear肯定有各种原因。另一方面，贵公司在企业领域发展得非常快，毕竟你们是新创公司。你们起步于中端市场，现在已经发展得很好了。所以，我觉得说它在企业领域行不通是不公平的。显然它运行得很好。虽然我不知道你们能否分享相关数据，但看起来进展不错，正在向高端市场扩展。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, growth has been good. Growth in enterprise has been leading the other segments because I think this year, especially we reached a tipping point where I think with software, so much of the buying decision is based on almost like a brand thing, like is this for us? A lot of times people pick "enterprise software." It's like, "Why? You know everyone doesn't want this," and they're like, "Yeah, but it's for us."
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得增长势头不错。企业业务板块的增长领跑了其他板块，因为我认为今年尤其如此——在软件领域，购买决策很大程度上取决于品牌效应。比如，人们会问：“这适合我们吗？”很多时候人们会选择“企业级软件”。但人们会反问：“为什么？毕竟不是所有人都需要这个啊。”对方就会回应：“对啊，但这就是为我们量身打造的。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You won't get fired for buying Microsoft or whatever.
turns.zh: 你买微软之类的产品又不会被炒鱿鱼。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, exactly, and I think that we're starting to have enough brand penetration amongst enterprises where people can have that feeling, right? They're like, "Hey, Linear is for us. Who are we? Well, we are a large company that wants to act like a startup." It's like, "Who doesn't want that? Who doesn't want to go fast?"
turns.zh: 是啊，说得太对了。我觉得我们在企业客户中的品牌影响力已经足够深厚，让他们能产生这种共鸣了。他们会说：“嘿，Linear就是为我们量身打造的。我们是谁？我们是一家想像初创公司一样运作的大型企业。”这就好比，“谁会不喜欢这样？谁不想快速发展？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I had Jeffrey Moore on the podcast, and this is exactly what crossing the chasm looks like. He talked about basically you need someone that's across the chasm like a later adopter that isn't the person that's, "I love new stuff, and I'm an early adopter kind of evangelist." You need someone that's like traditional old school, takes their time to start to adopt it for you to be like, "Oh, okay. Now, maybe I should really take it seriously."
turns.zh: 对啊。我在播客上邀请过杰弗里·摩尔，他说的就是“跨越鸿沟”的典型案例。他讲到，跨越鸿沟的人通常是后来者，不是那种“我爱新事物、是早期采用者的狂热者”的人。而是那些传统、保守、慢慢接受新事物的人，让别人觉得“哦，原来是这样，那或许我该认真考虑一下了。”

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: I also think that with this particular category of tool, and with a lot of other B2B software, not... Like no means not now, right? Not right now because it doesn't fit our budget. It doesn't fit our change management situation. "Oh, we have this exec that's really wedded to this other tool," but those things change, right? So, we keep in contact with them. They're in our CRM where we make sure we follow up, and we've had a lot of these where we've been said no to, like two years ago, and now we have some new features, and then go like, "Oh, yeah, it seems like you're ready for our scale," or whatever.
turns.zh: 我还觉得，对于这类工具，尤其是很多B2B软件，拒绝不代表现在不行，对吧？现在不行可能是因为预算不够，或者变革管理环境不允许，或者高管对现有工具太执着。但这些情况都会变，对吧？所以我们会和他们保持联系。他们在我们的CRM系统里，我们确保跟进。有很多两年前被拒绝的客户，现在我们推出了新功能，再去说：“哦，对啊，看来你们已经能承受我们的规模了”之类的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You mentioned that when you have these debates and questions that come out, you have features that a big company wants. There's this category of, "We know we will not build things for middle managers that want reporting and custom stuff just to track what's happening," versus something an IC wants to be more productive and successful, Linear. Give us a little sense of some of the more complicated debates that aren't necessarily in that bucket.
turns.zh: 你提到在讨论和提出问题时，我们有大企业需要的功能。还有一类是：“我们知道不会为只想报表和定制功能来追踪进展的中层管理者开发产品”，而另一类是IC希望提高生产力和成功率，比如Linear。能不能给我们讲讲那些不属于这两类的更复杂的讨论？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: I think the complicated debates are often when we do add a new native feature, do we extend an existing feature and make it more powerful or do we add a new sort of service? And a big part of that is trying to figure out exactly who's going to use it, what are the actual real life use cases that we know about? Like that I know that Bob from Company X has this workflow and this is how it would work for him. Here are the different variations where it would work. So, tying it all the way back to real people is-
turns.zh: 我觉得复杂的讨论通常在于：当我们添加新功能时，是扩展现有功能让它更强大，还是添加新服务？这很大程度上要搞清楚谁会用它，我们知道哪些真实的应用场景。比如我知道X公司的老鲍有这个工作流程，效果会这样。这里有各种变体方案。把一切都落实到真实用户身上——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Like a specific person?
turns.zh: 比如具体的人？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, specific person. Yeah. Yeah, exactly. Not a hypothetical person. Not one that you made up like Alice, Bob, or whatever. It's like, "No, here's the first name, last name. Here's their email. You can ask them," and I think that being able to tie it all the way back to reality in that way is a big part of how we really think about and discuss these things.
turns.zh: 是的，具体的人物。没错。就是这样，不是假设出来的某个人物，不是你虚构出来的爱丽丝、鲍勃之类的。而是，“不，这里有他们的名字、姓氏，还有邮箱。你可以去问问他们。”我觉得能以这种方式将一切与现实紧密相连，是我们真正思考和探讨这些问题的重要环节。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This connects the way I think about my newsletter is I always try to answer the question a very specific, like a person actually asked, not a general sense of something people may be interested in, and that very specific question, like it implies there's a need. Like not implies, it proves there's at least one person who needs this thing versus you have this idea of somebody that may want this thing.
turns.zh: 我对时事通讯的思考方式是，我总是试图回答一个非常具体的问题——比如某个人实际提出的问题，而不是人们可能感兴趣的某种笼统概念。那个非常具体的问题，意味着存在需求。不是暗示，而是证明至少有一个人需要这个东西，而不是你空想某个可能感兴趣的人。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah. I think a trap that a lot of times PMs will fall into is they'll make something, and they'll make some choices in it because maybe it's beautiful or it's elegant, but they don't go the step of like, "Is reality also beautiful and elegant?" Because reality is ugly sometimes, and if you have a beautiful and elegant solution that doesn't match with reality, it doesn't really matter. People can look at it, and they can ooh and ah, but if they don't use it to get their work done, it's never going to have long-term staying power.
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得很多产品经理常会陷入的一个误区是，他们会开发出某个东西，然后因为它设计得美观或优雅，就做出了某些决策，但他们却不去思考：“现实世界是否也美观优雅？”因为现实有时很丑陋。如果你设计出一个美观优雅的解决方案，却与现实不符，那就毫无意义。人们可能会赞叹不已，但如果他们无法用它来完成工作，它就永远无法获得长久的认可。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a heuristic of how often you need to hear something for you to... could be just convinced, this is worth investing in? People may hear this, "Oh, one Bob. Bob wants this featured." That doesn't make sense. It's just one guy. How do you know when it's like, "Okay, we should really invest in this"?
turns.zh: 你有没有一个经验法则，决定要听多少次某个说法才能……真正被说服，认为值得投入资源？比如有人说：“哦，鲍勃想要这个功能。”但这毫无意义。就一个鲍勃而已。怎样才能判断“好吧，我们真的应该投资这个功能”呢？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Part of it is you hear something, and you're like, "Gosh, that actually is... " Not only is that true. It means that the way we thought about this was a little bit wrong, and I call this process... I don't know if it's the right way to describe it. I call it a kneeling where you have a thing, and it's not quite the right shape, and you put it out into the wild. So, this happens way in the first bit of the life of a particular feature. You release a thing, and then you start getting feedback about it, about hey, it doesn't quite fit reality, and then you ask yourself like, "Did we test that aspect of it? Did we actually match that part to reality?" And if you didn't, then it's like that's the part where you don't actually need that many pieces of feedback against it. It's not really a volume thing. It's like, "Did we think about this right or wrong?" That's one sort of category. (00:27:01): Another category is just you're getting a request for maybe a very big feature or a feature set from a lot of different people, but then you dig in, and you try to say like, "Okay. Well, tell me about how you're trying to use this," and there's 100 different use cases. So, you have choices here. You can either build the big feature that covers all the long tail of use cases or you can try to see if there's really concentrated pools of use cases for this that really make a lot of sense to adopt as a first order type of feature. So, I think those are the two sort of strategies that we employ the most. It's like, "Did we think about this wrong? And now we're just learning something about how it matches reality or for this big general feature that people are asking for, are there actually more specific use cases that we should be solving, and we should be solving really, really well?"
turns.zh:
部分情况是，你听到某些信息后，会想：“天哪，事实上这确实是……” 这不仅仅是事实。这意味着我们对此的思考方式有些偏差。我把这个过程称为……我不知道用什么词来准确描述它。我称之为「下跪」——你开发出一个产品，但它的形状并不完全符合实际需求，然后就将其推向市场。这种情况往往发生在某个特定功能的早期阶段。你发布一个产品后，开始收到反馈，比如「这和现实不太符」，然后你会自问：「我们测试过这部分了吗？我们是否真正将这部分与现实相匹配了？」如果没有，那说明这部分其实不需要太多的反馈。关键不在于反馈的数量，而在于「我们对此的思考是否正确？」这属于第一类情况。

（00:27:01）：另一种情况是，你收到许多不同用户对某个大型功能或功能集的需求请求，但深入探究后，你会发现用户有100种不同的使用场景。面对这种情况，你可以有两个策略选择：要么构建一个涵盖所有长尾使用场景的大型功能，要么尝试找出其中真正高度集中的使用场景，将其作为优先级最高的功能进行开发。我认为这两种策略是我们最常用的。比如，「我们的思考是否有偏差？」以及「对于用户迫切需求的这个大型通用功能，是否存在更具体、需要我们深度解决的使用场景？」

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A thread that's coming through so far across a lot of these examples is getting to the specific person using the thing and making them happy and making sure the ask is going to solve their actual problem. In the case of looking at the IC versus the middle manager, in this case, it's like, "Let's talk to the person actually asking for this thing," not, "There's like 100 people generally asking for this thing and let's build what we think is a general solution."
turns.zh: 到目前为止，贯穿许多案例的一个核心思路是，真正了解使用产品的具体用户，满足他们的需求，确保所开发的产品能真正解决他们的实际问题。以IC与中层管理者的关系为例，关键在于：「让我们去和真正提出需求的人沟通」，而不是「有100个人普遍需要这个功能，那我们就去构建一个通用解决方案」。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah. I'll give you an example of all of these things, which we just launched a feature called Customer Requests, and basically what this does, it adds a new concept of Linear, which is a customer. For B2B companies, this is very relevant, and the reason we did this is because we kept getting this request for fully customized fields, and we would be like, "Well, what is it that you want with your custom fields?" Because the problem is you add 100 custom fields and all your ICs start hating it. So, we don't want to go down that path, but what is it actually you're trying to do? And 40% of them were because, "Well, I have a customer," like Walmart or whatever, right? Like, "Walmart asked for this feature, and it's really important. I need everyone to know that Walmart needs this. I need to track it. I need to see how have we report... " (00:29:09): We can report on what have we done for Walmart over the past year so that when my CSM has a one-on-one conversation with a rep, they can have some kind of evidence that we've been doing stuff for them, like all this kind of stuff. We're like, "Okay. Cool." That sounds like a very useful and powerful thing you want to do. How do you expect people to tag these things? Well, manually, because that's how we did it in our spreadsheets. It's like, "Okay, instead of that, we're going to hook up with your customer support tools. We're going to hook up with your CRNs. We're going to automatically bring in feedback from these companies. We're going to analyze the emails where they're from, and then if someone requests a feature that gets escalated into engineering, it'll just be tagged with whoever asked for it. You don't have to do anything, but you will know, and you can still report on this stuff, but there's nothing about this that makes ICs lives harder. (00:29:54): In fact, it makes them feel more confident because when they're building the thing, they actually understand who's asking for it and exactly what the email said. So, when they're doing the design or the details, they can actually see the real-life use cases that are present and solve for those directly.
turns.zh: 是的。我给你举个例子，我们刚推出了一个叫做“客户请求”的功能。它的核心功能是引入了一个新的概念——“客户线索（Linear）”。对于B2B公司来说，这非常实用。我们之所以推出这个功能，是因为不断收到用户关于完全自定义字段的请求。我们就会问：“你们到底想用这些自定义字段做什么？” 问题在于，一旦添加100个自定义字段，所有内部客户（IC）都会反感。所以我们不想走这条路，但用户真正想做的是什么？40%的请求是因为“我有客户”，比如沃尔玛之类的。他们会说：“沃尔玛需要这个功能，这非常重要。我需要让所有人知道沃尔玛需要这个功能。我需要跟踪进度……” （00:29:09）：我们可以汇报过去一年为沃尔玛做过哪些工作，这样当客户成功经理（CSM）与销售代表一对一沟通时，他们就能有证据证明我们一直在为他们服务，诸如此类的事情。我们觉得：“好的，这听起来是个很有用且强大的功能。你们打算怎么让用户标注这些内容呢？” 答：“手动标注，因为我们在电子表格中就是这么做的。” 我们说：“好吧，那我们要接入你们的客户支持工具和CRM系统，自动获取这些公司的反馈。然后分析邮件来自哪里，若某个功能请求被升级到工程部门，系统会自动标注提出请求的人。用户无需操作，但能随时查看反馈，而且这完全不会增加IC们的负担。” （00:29:54）：事实上，这让他们更有信心，因为在开发产品时，他们能清楚了解是谁提出的需求，以及邮件中的具体内容。这样一来，他们在设计和细节处理时就能直接参考真实的使用场景，直接解决问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: As I'm hearing this, it's like, "Okay, obviously, this seems like an obvious solution. Of course, 40% of people telling me they have customers." In reality, most of the time, if you hear from a bunch of your customers, "Hey, I need this custom field," and sometimes you hear one thing, sometimes you hear another. Most of the time you're going to build this custom field. Something that your head of sales shared with me is how impressed he is with the way you ask questions on customer calls and just keep digging and digging until you get to something that is an insight for you, and then you start to try to solve the problem for them and think about what the product might be, and I think this is such an important and underappreciated skill for PMs. Is there any advice you could share of just how you approach this, how you ask questions, how you think about these customer calls to get to, "Okay, now, I see what we need to build versus let's just build what they're asking for"?
turns.zh: 听你这么说，我觉得：“好的，显然这看起来是个显而易见的解决方案。果然，40%的人都说他们有客户。” 但现实中，大多数时候，如果你听到很多客户说：“嘿，我需要这个自定义字段”，然后有时听到一个说法，有时听到另一个。大多数时候你还是会去开发这个自定义字段。销售主管跟我分享过，他对你们在客户电话中提问的能力印象深刻——不断深挖，直到找到对你们有启发的洞察，然后开始尝试为他们解决问题，并思考产品可能的方向。我认为这对产品经理来说是一项非常重要但被低估的技能。你们有什么建议，能分享一下如何处理这些问题，如何提问，如何思考这些客户电话，从而得出“好的，现在我明白我们需要开发什么了，而不是简单地照用户说的做”？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: It's funny because I think from the outside, I'm on these sales calls and then the AE or someone's watching me ask these questions, and I think often they're like, "What are you doing? You're just asking questions from angles that I don't even know what your goal is here," and my goal is to feel bad in the same way that customers feel bad. They come to us with a request, "Hey, we want X," and it's like there's something motivating it and you can do the normal analytical thing and be like, "Ask five whys," and try to figure out like, "Well, what are your goals?" "And as a persona X, I want to achieve this outcome." You can do it that way, but you might miss the reason that they actually feel bad for not having this thing like, "I can't accomplish this goal. So what?" "So, I'm not going to get promoted at work." (00:31:44): Okay, great. I understand the severity of your problem at this point. What is the actual emotional valence that is motivating whatever you're telling me? And it takes a little while to get there. You can ask people directly like, "How do you feel?" And they're not necessarily going to tell you, but if you have a long enough and deep enough conversation with them, you start to level with them, and you're starting to see stuff from their perspective, and the more you see it from their perspective and the more they know that, the more they're willing to open up to you and tell you like, "Okay, honestly, I had this thing happen where I marked the ship date of this project as December 30th because it's a Q4 project, and I wanted to put it at the very end, and then my marketing team lost their mind because they're like, 'We can't ship something on December 30th. Everyone's on vacation,'" and you're like... And then they're like, "Yeah, this has made me feel really bad." (00:32:36): So, I don't ever want to put dates on things ever again. So, like, "Okay, cool. We can help you deal with that. If that's what you're feeling, then I can start building stuff to make sure that you never have to have that bad feeling again."
turns.zh: 这很有趣，因为从外部来看，我在参加销售电话会议时，AE（客户代表）或其他人会看着我问这些问题，他们常常会说：“你在干什么？你问的问题角度连我都不明白你的目的是什么。” 而我的目标是像客户感受到的那种糟糕情绪一样去体会他们的感受。客户来找我们时会说：“我们想要X。”这背后往往有某种驱动力，你可以用常规的分析方法，比如“五个为什么”，试图弄清楚他们的目标是什么，但你可能会忽略他们真正因为没有得到这项功能而感到糟糕的真正原因，比如“我无法达成这个目标。那又怎样？”“所以我升不了职了。” （00:31:44）：好的，我现在理解你问题的严重性了。那么，推动你讲述这些的实际情感倾向是什么？要找到这个需要花些时间。你可以直接问人们：“你感觉如何？”但他们不一定会告诉你。但如果你和他们进行足够深入的对话，你会逐渐与他们达成共鸣，从他们的角度看问题。当他们越能从你的角度理解问题，就越愿意向你敞开心扉，比如：“好吧，说实话，我曾把这个项目的交付日期定为12月30日，因为这是第四季度的项目，我想把它放在最后，结果我的营销团队暴跳如雷，他们说：‘12月30日根本没法交付，人人都放假了。’” 而你会回应：“是啊，这让我感觉糟透了。” （00:32:36）：所以，我再也不想给任何事情设定截止日期了。所以，比如：“好的，没关系。我们可以帮你解决这个问题。如果这就是你的感受，那我可以开始搭建工具，确保你再也不必有这种糟糕的感觉了。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: People talk about empathy like, "You need to have empathy as a PM. You need to build empathy the best product leaders, have empathy in this." I think it's such a succinct and powerful way of describing what empathy actually looks like as a product leader, which is I want to feel as bad as they feel in hearing the story they tell, and it sounds like the way you do that is you keep asking questions to understand the moment they felt bad about something. In this case, the deadline.
turns.zh: 人们谈论同理心时会说：“作为产品经理，你需要有同理心。你需要成为最具同理心的产品领导者，在这件事上要具备同理心。” 我认为这是一种简洁而有力的方式，描述了产品领导者真正需要具备的同理心，那就是在听客户讲述他们的故事时，要感受到他们所感受到的糟糕情绪。而实现这一点的方法，就是不断提问，理解他们感到糟糕的那个瞬间。在这个案例中，就是截止日期。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: And if you ask somebody in that last story, like what kind of issue do you have? You're like, "Oh, marketing and I would just never align on anything." It's like that doesn't really tell you what's going on. What it tells you is you had this terrible moment of communication that it's all miscommunicated, and you're like, "It's just going to keep happening over and over again." So, the thing that we did specifically to solve this was on projects in Linear, you can just specify a target date at whatever level of granularity you want. You can say it's a December project. You can say it's a Q4 project. You can say it's a second half of 2024 project. Like whatever you're happy promising, you can just put it on there and that way you never feel like you have to give this sense of false precision so that it ends up with a whole bunch of miscommunication down the line.
turns.zh: 如果你问那个故事中的人：“你遇到了什么问题？”他们可能会说：“哦，营销部门和我永远无法达成共识。” 但这并不能真正告诉你问题的根源。它只告诉你，你们之间有过糟糕的沟通，信息传达不清，而你会说：“这种情况只会一次又一次地发生。” 所以，我们专门为此做出的改进是在Linear平台上的项目中，你可以根据需要指定任意粒度的目标日期。你可以说这是12月的项目。可以说这是第四季度的项目。可以说这是2024年下半年的项目。只要你愿意承诺，你就可以把日期设定在那里，这样你就不必给出虚假的精确度，最终导致一堆沟通不畅的问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I could see why people love Linear is it just makes them feel less bad less often. There's a lot of connection here. I know this idea of emotions and feeling bad is a core part of how you think about building product, looking for moments. People feel bad. Is there anything more you could share there to share how you think about this idea of emotional hooks, emotional moments, and how you decide what to build?
turns.zh: 我能理解人们为何钟爱 Linear——它只是能让人们更少感到沮丧、更少陷入负面情绪。这种情感共鸣在这里非常明显。我知道，你在产品设计时把情感和负面情绪视为核心考量，致力于捕捉关键触发点。人们难免会情绪低落。你能否分享更多心得，谈谈如何设计情感钩子和情感触点，如何筛选出值得开发的功能？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: So, to set the background of this, I've worked in very, very competitive industries. I worked at Everlane, which was a direct-to-consumer clothing brand. I worked in Mode, which is like BI tools and there's so many BI tools out there, and then obviously, Linear. We're project management. There's a lot of project management tools, and I think the more competitive your industry is, the more the low-hanging goal-oriented stuff is already picked because every PM from every one of these companies has been asking like, "Well, what's your goal? What is your job to be done," and all this kind of stuff. So, you have to look at things from an angle that other people might not have seen and for me, and for us, it's the angle of where are the emotional hooks that you're experiencing as you go through your work day, as you use our product, as you use competitors' products? (00:35:21): I think it's probably underexplored because... I don't know. I feel like PMs and engineers, we're like very thinky people. We avoid the touchy-feely stuff. So, I think that's the opportunity. You can see where are you feeling bad throughout your day where you don't even know? You might think, "I hate Mondays." "Why do you hate Mondays?" "Well, on Mondays, I have to go out and gather a whole bunch of stuff to write this report that it's really annoying." "Oh, so if I gave you a button that made the report, would that help?" It's like, "Oh, yeah, then I might not hate Monday so much." So, I think Paul Graham has a word for this. He calls it schlep blindness, right? It's like I'm schlepping through life, and I'm just completely blind to it, and it's true. You have to have an outsider come in and see what the rhythm of your feelings are throughout the day, throughout the week, and you note the spots where you could really use a lot of improvement.
turns.zh: 先讲背景吧，我曾在竞争激烈的行业工作过。曾在直销服装品牌 Everlane任职，之后转战 BI 工具领域（Mode 公司），现在专注于项目管理（Linear）。这些行业竞争越激烈，低垂的目标导向型功能往往被迅速采纳，因为每个公司的项目经理都会反复追问：“你的目标是什么？你的工作重点是什么？” 之类的问题。所以，你必须从别人未曾触及的角度思考。对我和团队而言，关键在于：用户在日常工作中、使用产品时、对比竞品时，会经历哪些负面情绪触点？（00:35:21）我觉得这方面的探索还不够深入……我不知道。项目经理和工程师通常比较理性，回避感性话题。这正是突破口所在。你能发现用户日常哪些时刻情绪低落却未被察觉？比如“我讨厌周一。”“为什么？”“因为周一要收集资料写报告，太烦人了。”“那如果有个按钮能自动生成报告呢？”用户会说：“太棒了，这样我就不会讨厌周一了。” 保罗·格雷厄姆称这种现象为“盲目拖延”（schlep blindness）。这就像我们在生活中机械地前行，却对情绪波动视而不见。确实如此。你需要一个局外人来洞察用户每日、每周的情绪节奏，指出可以优化的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example? I've shared a couple, but just where you've noticed this in someone using maybe a competitor or even Linear that you solved. I know you gave an example of the dates. I guess is there anything else?
turns.zh: 能举个例子吗？我分享过几个案例，但想听你讲讲用户使用竞争对手产品或 Linear 时解决问题的案例。我记得你提到日期管理的例子。还有其他案例吗？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: A big feature that people love about Linear is we have this thing called Triage Management, and what it does is it systemizes this thing where if I put an issue into a different team, if I'm asking them to do something or I'm reporting a bug to them, it sticks in a special zone where it'll notify the right people. They're on a rotation and people will be able to respond to it in an organized manner, and I think this kind of automation, this feature, it came out of two different fields people were having. One, people were trying to implement this stuff by hand, and it was just a lot of touches, and they were doing it, but they felt like, "Oh, I'm totally underwater." "Why are you under water?" "Well, I have to throw all these tickets around and route them correctly and stuff like that," and they didn't see this as an opportunity to have a tool specialize in managing their triage queue. (00:37:23): Because they were managing by hand.... They were on top of it, but it just felt really bad because they just had to spend so much attention doing this and then there's the folks who didn't do that. The feeling was just like, "Well, it's totally out of control. People are just throwing tickets over the wall, and I don't know what to do with them. I don't know where they are. They end up in all these holes and then the people on the other side are like, "I throw tickets over the wall. I have no idea what happens to them. I have no expectation that people are ever going to respond to them." So, there's all of these bad feelings that people are having. They all have the same root cause, which is like there wasn't a very automated organized way to deal with your triage queue.
turns.zh:
关于 Linear 的一项深受用户喜爱的功能是我们推出的"分诊管理"系统。该功能通过将问题归类至不同团队来实现系统化管理。例如，当我向某个团队提交问题、请求协助或上报漏洞时，系统会自动将这些任务归入专属区域，并及时通知相关人员。团队成员会按照轮班制进行处理，确保问题得到有条不紊的响应。

开发这项功能的灵感源于两个领域的痛点：一是手动管理的繁琐——用户曾尝试通过人工方式处理这些任务，但发现效率低下，总被各种琐事拖累；二是缺乏专业化工具支持分诊队列管理。（00:37:23）由于当时团队仍采用手动管理模式，虽然表面上井井有条，但实际效率极低。另一部分用户则完全束手无策，问题如雪片般飞来却无从下手。

归根结底，问题的核心在于缺乏自动化分诊工具来规范管理流程。借助 Linear 的分诊管理系统，团队能够将分诊流程标准化，提升整体协作效率，同时避免信息遗漏和沟通障碍。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Marketers, I know that you love TLDRs. So, let me get right to the point. Wix Studio gives you everything you need to cater to any client at any scale, all in one place. Here's how your workflow could look. Scale content with dynamic pages and reusable assets effortlessly. Fast-track projects with built-in marketing integrations like Meta, CAPI, Zapier, Google Ads, and more. A-B test landing pages in days, not weeks with intuitive design tools. Connect to tracking and analytics tools like Google Analytics and Semrush, and capture key business events without the hassle of manual setup. Manage all your client's social media and communications from a unified dashboard, then create schedule and post content across all their channels. If you're on content-rich sites, Wix Studio's no-code CMS lets you build and manage without touching the design. And when you're ready for more, Wix Studio grows with you. Add your own code, create custom integrations with Wix-made APIs, or leverage robust native business solutions. Drive real client growth with Wix Studio. Go to wixstudio.com. (00:38:55): I'm going to try to summarize some of the secrets of Linear's success so far. So, the first is get something out as quickly as possible, say, in the first 10% of the time that you have to build this thing and get it out to internal users and then maybe a growing list of beta users and people that are aware of they're using early stuff. Two is prioritize the IC and the user, basically, versus the buyer or the middle manager that wants reporting and all these custom features. So, it's basically focused on the user, which I think you hear a lot, but I love this very specific example. Three is when you hear asks for features and requests, get to the specific person using the thing, not just general, "Okay, cool. I've heard it 100 times." Find the person that actually needs this thing and understand what's going on, and then four is look for people feeling bad in a moment working in the product. Is there anything else that I'm missing that's important or any nuance you want to add?
turns.zh:
营销人员们，我知道你们喜欢简洁明了的总结。所以，让我直接切入正题。Wix Studio为您提供了一站式解决方案，助您满足任何规模客户的需求。以下是您的创作流程可能呈现的模样：  
- 通过动态页面和可重复利用的素材轻松扩展内容。  
- 借助内置的营销集成（如Meta、CAPI、Zapier、Google Ads等）快速推进项目。  
- 利用直观的设计工具，在数日而非数周内完成着陆页A/B测试。  
- 无缝对接Google Analytics和Semrush等追踪分析工具，无需手动设置即可捕捉关键业务事件。  
- 通过统一仪表板管理所有客户的社交媒体与沟通渠道，并跨全渠道安排内容发布。  
- 若您需要内容丰富的网站，Wix Studio的无代码CMS让您无需触及设计即可构建和管理内容。  
- 当您准备好更深入的功能时，Wix Studio会与您共同成长。添加自定义代码、利用Wix自有API创建定制集成，或借助强大的原生商业解决方案。  
- 借助Wix Studio推动客户真实增长。访问wixstudio.com。  

（00:38:55）：接下来，我想总结一下Linear迄今为止成功的秘诀。首先，尽快推出产品。比如，在构建产品的前10%时间内，将产品交付给内部用户，然后再扩展到越来越多的测试用户和了解早期版本的用户。  
第二，优先考虑内部客户（IC）和用户，而不是希望获得报告和定制功能的采购方或中层管理者。  
第三，当听到功能请求时，要找到实际使用该产品的用户，而非一概而论地说“好的，酷，我听过100次了”。要找到真正需要该功能的人，并理解他们的需求。  
第四，留意产品使用过程中用户可能遇到的困境。  
还有什么重要之处或细微差别需要补充吗？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: The part where you said, like focus on the user, I think it's maybe a little bit more subtle than that. There's a nuance which is find where the incentives are really misaligned amongst your user base. There's a middle manager that wants really detailed reporting and there's a IC who just really doesn't want to go through all those extra steps, and the incentives for what they want are just very... They're just very misaligned, and you have to find those situations and be pretty judicious about how you make those trade-offs and where you can really find win-win outcomes there.
turns.zh: 您提到要关注用户，但我认为这可能需要更深入的理解。比如，要找到用户群体中激励机制严重不一致的情况。有些中层管理者希望获得详细的报告，而内部客户却不愿经历这些额外步骤，他们的需求动机严重不一致。您需要识别这些情况，并谨慎处理权衡取舍，找到双赢的解决方案。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really important nuance. Something else that's come through a couple of times as you've been talking is also something Patrick Collison tweeted once that has stuck with me, which is this idea of having a mental model in your head of the user. So, the way he described it and the way you've described it is oftentimes people are like, "Cool. We're going to figure out what to build. We're going to do a bunch of research, talk to users. That'll inform what we build, and we build it, versus what you've been saying and what he said is you do a bunch of research, look at data, talk to people. That informs your mental model of what the customer needs in their life, and then that informs what you build. So, that anytime you do more research, talk to customers, it's informing your view of the person, and then you're like, "Oh, this was different from what I imagined," or, "Oh wow. This is exactly what we've been thinking and let's build that." Anything along those lines that you might want to share?
turns.zh: 这确实是一个很重要的细节。在你们的讨论中，我还注意到帕特里克·科利森（Patrick Collison）曾在推特上提到的一个观点，一直让我印象深刻，那就是要在脑海中建立起用户的心理模型。他描述的思路和你所说的很相似——通常人们会想：“好吧，我们要先调研用户需求，再收集数据、与用户交流，这些信息会指导我们的产品设计。” 而你所说的方法是，先深入研究、收集数据、与用户沟通，这些信息会形成你对用户生活需求的心理模型，进而指导产品设计。每当你进行更多调研、与用户交流时，都会更新对用户的认知，可能发现“原来情况和我们想象的不一样”，或者“哇，这正是我们一直在思考的，赶紧把它实现吧”。你能否分享一下类似的经验？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, I can tell you a little bit about how we manage our backlog, which I think actually ties directly into this. At any given moment, we have probably 20 or 30 opportunities that we could possibly explore, just product opportunities, like problems to solve, areas to improve for our users, but they're not ready yet. We don't have enough conviction around how we might approach it. So, we just accumulate understanding of this stuff and periodically, we accumulate some more stuff, and then we reevaluate, "Okay, what is our current understanding of how we might best approach this thing?" And I think something that people struggle with is that they might have this model in their head. Like a PM might have this model in their head about how a user behaves, but it's just very hard to share that with someone else. You have to telepathically throw it into their brain, which is hard. So, what we try to do is identify areas that we might attack with a product, but also keep an up-to-date analysis of each of those areas so that everyone can engage with it and also contribute.
turns.zh: 好的，我可以简单讲讲我们如何管理产品待办事项列表，我觉得这和你的问题直接相关。目前，我们大概有20到30个可能探索的机会，都是产品层面的机会，比如需要解决的问题、提升用户体验的领域，但这些想法还不够成熟。我们对如何推进这些项目没有足够的信心。因此，我们会持续收集相关信息，定期整合新内容，然后重新评估：“目前我们对如何最好地推进这个项目有何理解？”我认为很多人会遇到的一个难题是，他们脑海中可能有某种模型，比如产品经理对用户行为的假设，但很难与他人分享这些模型。你得把这些想法神秘地植入对方脑中，实在太难了。所以我们尝试的方法是，确定可能开展产品攻势的领域，同时对每个领域保持动态分析，这样每个人都能参与进来并贡献力量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Is there an example of something that's sitting in your roadmap? I don't know if you could share these sort of things that's just sitting in the backlog of just like, "We're not quite ready to tackle this yet, but here's something we're inkling on."
turns.zh: 有没有正在路线图上的例子？不知道你能否分享一些待办事项列表中的项目，比如“我们现在还没准备好着手这个，但这是我们正在考虑的方向”之类的。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, sure. Capacity planning is a thing that's been sitting in our backlog, and it's something that we see managers struggle with all the time, which is like I have a limited amount of personnel and resources, and I need to deploy them in such a way where we can theoretically accomplish our roadmap, but also we don't get blocked by some bottleneck that we don't end up blocking all of the projects because this one engineer is stuck on some info thing, and that's a thing people struggle with all the time. All the solutions out there are bad. The best solution is a very, very custom spreadsheet that someone would make, and it's a lot of upkeep. So, we have some ideas about how we might automate this, how we might use existing data within Linear to really help out with this problem, but I don't think we've quite cracked it yet. (00:43:18): I think there's some nuances that we have to really explore a little bit further. So, we're continuously developing this, and as we hear from hear from users that are struggling with this problem, we will get on a call with them and sit down with them and talk through it.
turns.zh:
是的，没错。产能规划是我们积压已久的一个任务，也是管理者们长期面临的难题——比如我手头的人力和资源有限，需要合理分配，以便既能按计划推进项目，又不会因某个工程师卡在某个技术细节上而导致整个项目停滞。这确实是个老大难问题。

市面上的解决方案都不尽如人意。最好的办法是建立一个定制化的电子表格，但维护成本太高。所以我们一直在探索如何实现自动化管理，如何利用 Linear 现有的数据来解决这个难题，但目前还没有完全攻克。（00:43:18）：我们需要进一步挖掘其中的细节。为此，我们持续开发相关功能，并在用户反馈中不断优化，帮助他们更高效地应对挑战。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And the idea there is keep informing this mental model, keep informing what this could be until you get to a place of like, "Okay. Cool. I think we figured out what will really solve this problem in an elegant way"?
turns.zh: 关键在于不断完善这个思维模型，不断探索可能的解决方案，直到最终找到一个既优雅又切实可行的方案。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, and I want to really stress a nuance here, which is it's not that we want to solve the entire problem. The entire problem is quite big, but there's something that's really right for Linear to do that would help people have a good starting point for them to reason about it. So, I think a lot of building conviction around stuff is not even like do we have a workable solution? It's like how much of the problem should we actually take on? Because if we take on too much of the problem, then we'll end up overpromising and not being able to deliver on it.
turns.zh: 是的，我特别想强调一点，我们的目标不是解决整个难题。整个问题太庞大了，但 Linear 可以着手解决的部分，足以为用户提供一个良好的入手点，让他们能够理性思考。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think what's also useful here is you all keep your team very small intentionally and being constrained keeps you from taking on these things too early because you don't have the engineers to build their designers.
turns.zh: 这里还有个有用的点是，我们故意保持团队规模较小，受限的环境反而能避免过早承担过多任务，因为我们没有足够的工程师和设计师来支持这些项目。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, that's true. I actually hadn't really put that part together, but I think some of the reason we've done it this way is because we don't have the bandwidth to action everything. So, we have this backlog that we maintain to make sure that when we do take it on, we're pretty set up for success.
turns.zh: 没错，确实如此。我之前没有意识到这一点，但我们之所以采取这种方式，部分原因是我们没有足够的资源去全面推进所有项目。因此，我们通过积压列表来控制节奏，确保一旦接手项目，就能做好充分准备。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, it's interesting. I think a lot of companies are starting to realize that they can build better products and move faster with fewer teams. I want to move in a different direction and talk a bit about how you actually think about building new products. Something that I've heard from you is that you have a systemized way of being creative, which I think is a dream for a lot of people's. It's like how do I be more creative? How do I think of new innovative concepts? You have a really interesting process for how you do this. Can you talk about it?
turns.zh: 是的，这很值得思考。我发现很多公司开始意识到，利用更精简的团队也能打造出更优质的产品，推进速度更快。我想转换一下话题，谈谈你们如何构思新产品。我听说你们有系统化的创新方法，这对很多人来说简直是梦想。如何提高创造力？如何产生创新理念？你们的流程非常有趣，能否分享一下？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, totally. I think when people talk about being creative, a lot of times what they have a problem with is extrapolating. They can see the stuff that's right in front of them, but what about two or three steps down the line? And then it's just like, "Well, there's just so much possibility. I don't know what direction to go." So, the way that we try to do it is we ask a question which is like, "Okay, how extreme can you take it? You're designing a product. You're trying to come up with a solution. What's the most outrageous version of this along some trait?" I don't know if you guys did this at Airbnb, but I think Brian Chesky talks about like, "What's the 11-star experience?" Is that a thing you guys did?
turns.zh: 是的，完全赞同。我觉得人们在谈论创造力时，很多时候面临的难题是无法跳出固有思维。他们能看到眼前的东西，但再往下想两三步呢？然后就会陷入困境，"天哪，可能性太多了，真不知道该往哪个方向走。"所以我们的做法是这样的，我们会问一个问题："好吧，你能把它推向极致吗？你正在设计一款产品，试图找到解决方案。那么在某个特定维度上，最极端的版本会是怎样的？"不知道你们在Airbnb有没有这样做，但布莱恩·切斯基曾提到过"11星级体验"。这是你们做过的吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It was a thing he talked about. Yeah, there's always a push of what's the 10X version of some idea.
turns.zh: 他确实提过这个。是啊，总有人会追问某个想法能极端到什么程度。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: When you think in that way, when you're saying like, "Hey, what's the 11-star experience?" What you're really asking is like, "Hey, what's the most luxurious version of this hotel stay? Or what's the most unforgettable kind of experience we can give people?" And you throw away things, I don't know, like cost. You throw away things like practicality because that's not what's interesting. What's interesting is I want to actually explore the possibility space, and I think this is really important to do because the goal is to get you to see beyond your defaults. We have all of these constraints that we're operating under that we psychically have in the back of our heads that we just don't even realize we have them. So, just break past all of them, and then you can really see what your options are because we talk about product decisions. It's like, "Oh, yeah, you have these choices. What are you going to decide?" There's all this decision-making kind of theory. (00:46:52): But the biggest risk is you didn't see the right choice to begin with. You have these three choices and none of them were right. It's this fourth one that was over in this corner, but you didn't look in that corner, so you never found it. So, I think the whole goal of this is to try to expand the search space of what you're trying to do.
turns.zh: 当你以这种方式思考时，当你问"嘿，11星级体验是什么？"实际上你问的是"这家酒店住宿能有多奢华？"或者"我们能给人们带来多难忘的体验？"你抛开成本之类的因素，也不考虑实用性，因为那些才没意思。真正有趣的是去探索可能的空间。我觉得这很重要，因为目标是让你突破固有思维。我们的工作中总有这样的决策时刻："哦，对啊，你有这些选择，该选哪个？"这背后有整个决策理论。（00:46:52）但最大的风险是，一开始你就没选对。三个选项都不合适，而第四个选项就在角落里，但你没去看那个角落，所以永远找不到它。所以我觉得整个关键在于试图扩大你正在做的事情的搜索空间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, what you're saying is people often don't think out of the box enough by not thinking too radically enough. So, the choices they're deciding between are just meh options and there's this process of breaking out of that, and I think you could hear this and be like, "Yeah, sure." I could spend 10 minutes being like, "Oh, hey, what's the craziest [inaudible 00:47:35]- "
turns.zh: 所以你的意思是人们往往因为不够大胆而无法跳出固有思维。所以他们做出的选择只是平庸的选项，而突破这一局限的过程很重要。我想你们听了可能会觉得"是啊，当然。"我可以花10分钟说"哦，嘿，最疯狂的[00:47:35不清]-"

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But you're saying that actually is what you do and that actually works really well?
turns.zh: 但你说这确实是你们的做法，而且效果很好？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, and you actually build it. You can think of a very extreme version of a product and you can say, "Hey, let's actually... " For the first version, we talked about, like the first version, you know it's not really the right answer. Sometimes, you know it's so hard because you know this is the most extreme version of the answer. So, let's build that as fast as we can and see how it feels, and then we're going to learn so much about what the right actual answer is because we have seen this area of the product space and really felt it.
turns.zh: 是的，而且你们真的会把它做出来。你们可以构想一个产品的极端版本，然后说"嘿，咱们先把它做出来..."对于第一个版本，我们谈到，第一版本其实不是正确答案。有时候，知道这是最极端的版本会让人很头疼。所以我们尽快把它做出来，看看感觉如何，然后就能从中了解到正确的实际答案，因为我们已经探索了产品的这个领域，并且真正感受到了它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Let's talk about an example of this because this feels awesome.
turns.zh: 太棒了。那我们来举个例子吧，因为这听起来很棒。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, I can talk to an example. Actually, is it okay if I demo something?
turns.zh: 是的，我可以举个例子。其实，您介意我演示一下吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. Let's do it. Show and tell.
turns.zh: 当然没问题。开始吧。边演示边讲解。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, let me do that right now.
turns.zh: 好的，我现在就来做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Here we go. We're going to share screen.
turns.zh: 开始吧。我们要共享屏幕了。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: All right. So, this is just like a demo space instead of Linear. So, the feature where we did this that I remember very clearly, because it was recent, is we built this feature to save drafts for your issues. So, Linear, as hard as an issue tracker, if I make a new issue and let's say I'm trying to report a bug or something, so it's like I make a bug report, then I might start thinking through like, "Okay, what are the repro steps?" And then I start typing them, and this happens all the time. When you're at work, you're doing this and someone distracts you. If someone pings you on Slack or you have to go to a meeting or something like that, you're like, "I got to put this away for a second. I'll come back to it later." Note to self, figure out the actual repro steps and do it. (00:48:56): So, what can you do? Well, you want to save it as a draft. So, we're like, "Okay, this is the problem," and the first version of this, we're like, "What do we want to do? Linear is about being fast." So, we don't want to get in your way. We want to say like, "What is the fastest draft saving experience possible?" So, if you save it as draft, you can save it as draft. If you decide to not... you want to throw it away, you don't want it, just hit the X button, and it'll just throw it away. We're not going to interrupt you with a popup that says like, "Do you want to save your changes," or any of that kind of stuff. We'll just absolutely get out of your way fast as possible. So, we're like, "What's the risk here?" Well, it might feel really unsafe. (00:49:31): If you close this, and we don't ask you if you want to save change, you might feel like, "Oh, I just lost my changes on accident." We knew that going in. We built this anyway, and it felt super unsafe. It turns out that sort of inkling that we had was true, and we really felt exactly how unsafe it was. So, then we were like, "Okay, well, what's the safest thing we could possibly do?" The safest thing is just auto save everything. So, you start a new issue, and then you start typing some stuff, and it's just like auto saving as soon as you type a single character and that did feel quite safe. So, cool, but it also ended up leaving behind a whole bunch of like a paper trail of things you change your mind about. You've probably had this happen in document tools where you have a whole bunch of things in your space called like Untitled Document or New Document and stuff like that. It's just like-
turns.zh: 好的。这里是示例空间，不是 Linear。所以，我记得最近做的一个功能，就是为问题草稿保存功能。Linear 作为一个问题跟踪工具，虽然很实用，但比如我新建一个问题，要报告一个 bug 之类的，首先要构思重现步骤，然后开始输入，这时候总会被打断。工作时，有人找你，或者 Slack 消息提醒，或者要开会之类的，就得先放下手头工作。（00:48:56）那怎么办呢？保存为草稿啊。比如我们想，"好吧，这是个痛点"。第一版时，我们思考，"怎么做最简洁？Linear 讲究高效"，所以不想增加用户负担，直接提供最快速的草稿保存体验。保存为草稿后，再决定是否丢弃，直接点击 X 按钮即可。不会弹出提示让你保存更改之类的，尽可能不打断用户。（00:49:31）但用户可能觉得不安全。关闭页面却没提示保存，可能会误删。我们预料到这种情况，还是做了。结果发现这种担忧是合理的，用户确实会感到不安。于是我们决定最安全的做法就是自动保存。新建问题后输入内容，系统会实时保存草稿，这样既安全又方便。不过用户可能会留下很多草稿文件夹，比如 Untitled Document 之类的，这也挺烦人的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So many untitled folders.
turns.zh: 好多未命名文件夹啊。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, so many untitled folders because the moment you say new folder, it starts saving it, and then you don't actually mean for that to happen. So, we had those two sorts of variations that we built, and we fell through and where we ended up was a balance between those two. So, what happens is if I'm creating a new issue, like I am here, and I close it out, it'll interrupt me, like we have to interrupt you, otherwise it feels too unsafe. So, I can save the draft, I can go to my drafts, and then if I'm in this draft I've already made, and I go in there, and I start to say, "Okay, I'm going to keep working on it," but then I get interrupted again, then I'm just going to auto-save it for you. There's no point. I'm not going to ask you again. (00:51:06): I'm always going to auto save it because I'm not going to create a new object. I'm just making modifications in place. So, we made this very specific choice of on a brand new issue, we will interrupt you, and then on an existing draft that you're messing around with, we're just going to auto save everything and someone doing a analysis. If they did a detailed teardown of these decisions, they might say like, "Wow, they made very specific choices here," but the path to get there is to do something totally extreme in one direction and then totally extreme in another direction and then find where they really meet up.
turns.zh: 是啊，有那么多未命名的文件夹，因为当你说要新建文件夹时，它就开始保存了，而你其实并不想这样。所以，我们开发了两种解决方案，最后折中选择了两者的平衡。举个例子，如果我现在正在创建一个新问题，然后关闭它，系统会打断我，因为我们必须打断用户，否则体验会太不安全。所以我可以保存草稿，进入草稿列表，查看已有的草稿，再开始继续编辑，但又会被打断。这时候系统就会自动保存草稿，没有必要再询问用户了。（00:51:06）：我会一直自动保存草稿，因为我不需要创建新对象，只是在原有内容上进行修改。所以我们做出了这样的具体选择：在全新的问题上打断用户，而在用户正在修改的现有草稿上，则自动保存所有内容，并让分析人员使用。如果有人详细剖析这些决策，可能就会感叹：“哇，他们在这里做出了非常具体的选择。”但达成这一结果的路径，就是在一个方向上走向极端，再在另一个方向上走向极端，然后找到它们真正交汇的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a good example, the way that you described it is you went like here's the safest route. Here's the fastest version. Where did you come up with these list of options? And for folks that are trying to do this for their company, are these like... Because these are Linear principles, we're going to be very fast. Is this the way you think most companies should operate these sorts of attributes? Do you think it's specific to what makes their product different? How do you think about that?
turns.zh: 你举的这个例子太棒了。你描述的方式就是先找到最安全的路径，再找到最快的版本。这些选项列表是从哪里来的？对于那些想为公司做这类事情的人来说，这些是否……因为这些都是 Linear 原则，我们要做到极快。你认为大多数公司应该按照这些原则运营吗？你觉得这只是 Linear 的特定属性吗？你怎么看？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: I think for a lot of companies, you have to ask, "What is the promise that your product or your business is making people?" It might be you always have a car available if you need it, and if you do that, then maybe we're going to have to implement search pricing to make that happen. It's always going to be available. So, here's the trade-off that we have to make. It's a very extreme point of view to do that. Or you might say the price is always predictable, but sometimes you can't have a car in the first place. Those are all choices that you get to make, and you have to sort decide, like where in that spectrum does it make sense based on the promise of your company?
turns.zh: 我认为对于很多公司，你必须问：“你的产品或业务向用户做出了什么承诺？”可能是你需要时总能有车可用，如果要实现这一点，可能就需要实施搜索定价机制。它必须随时可用。所以这就是我们必须做出的权衡。这是一个非常极端的观点。但你也可以说，价格始终可预测，但有时你根本就无法提供车辆。这些都是你可以做出的选择，你必须决定，根据公司的承诺，在这个范围的哪一端更有意义？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A lot of people talk about this idea of working backwards. Brian Chesky in Airbnb has a big concept of working backwards from the ideal. Let's design the best possible scenario and work backwards. I love that this is even more tactical, which is just pick the extreme version of very specific attributes. Probably not that ideal, but it'll give us insight into a version of the ideal and an element that works well and then what doesn't. Yeah, exactly. I did this a lot actually at Airbnb, just like testing the extreme. So, it super resonates, this idea, and when you say test, so was it like you build it and play with it? Do you roll it out to some of these circles of users or is it often just internal, and then you learn and then iterate?
turns.zh: 很多人谈论逆向工程的理念。Airbnb 的布莱恩·切斯基有一个从理想状态出发逆向工程的宏大理念。让我们设计出最佳场景，然后逆向推导。我喜欢这种更具策略性的方法，即选择特定属性的极端版本。可能不那么理想，但它能让我们洞察理想版本的要素，哪些有效，哪些无效。是的，确实如此。我在 Airbnb 也经常这样做，就是测试极端版本。所以我对这个理念深有共鸣。当你说测试时，比如是构建后测试用户吗？还是会向一些用户群体推出？通常都是内部测试，然后再学习并迭代？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, we rolled out some of these versions to people.
turns.zh: 是的，我们向一些用户推出了这些版本。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, wow. Okay.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。好吧。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: So, the super-fast version that was unsafe, that only went interna, and everyone felt it was too unsafe, but then we thought, "Okay, let's go to the super-safe version," and then we rolled that out and everyone started having a whole bunch of... Like how many drafts are people making? I'm like, "This is too many." The people are leaving behind this crazy paper trail. Okay, we got to figure out some difference here.
turns.zh: 所以，之前那个速度超快但不安全的版本，只在内部使用，每个人都觉得太不安全了。但后来我们想，"好吧，那就用超级安全的版本吧。"然后我们推出了这个版本，结果大家又开始做一堆……比如，人们到底做了多少个草稿？我觉得这太多了。这些人留下了大量不必要的文档记录。好吧，我们得想办法解决这个问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. So, this very much connects to your first point of get things out really quick, and in this case, it's like extreme versions. You're probably not going to work long term, but it will teach you.
turns.zh: 太棒了。所以，这和你的第一个观点——尽快把事情做出来——非常契合。在这种情况下，就是要尝试极端的版本。你可能短期内用不上，但这能让你学到东西。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 是啊，就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Okay, and seeing it in action, I'm like, "Okay, obviously, this is the solution," and that's how the way this should feel, and to your point, it was not an obvious solution when you started thinking about it.
turns.zh: 太棒了。好吧，看它实际运行起来，就觉得，"显然，这就是解决方案。"这才是应该有的体验，正如你所说，一开始你可能没想明白。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, the best solutions are always obvious in hindsight, and it's just like you have to develop a process internally that to eventually find your way there.
turns.zh: 是啊。我是说，最好的解决方案往往在事后看来显而易见，你得在内部建立一个流程，最终才能找到正确的方向。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something else that you've mentioned when we were chatting that connects to some of the things we've been talking about is you have this perspective that B2B software isn't just solving people's problems, it's also teaching them how to work, and it's this accumulation of information. Can you talk about that? Because I thought that was really fascinating.
turns.zh: 我们之前聊天时，你提到过一个观点，这和我们讨论的内容有关，那就是B2B软件不只是解决人们的问题，还要教会他们如何工作，这是一个信息积累的过程。你能详细说说吗？因为我觉得这真的很吸引人。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: If you think about how a lot of B2B software gets created, it's because there was some person in the middle of some giant company who implemented some kind of process, and they're like, "Wow, this process is really working for us. Maybe we should make it easier," and they build a little tool internally and then all of their colleagues can now press on buttons and good things happen, and then they turn that process and that tool. They spin it off into a startup, and they make a startup. This process repeats thousands of times. So, when you adopt that tool, you're not just adopting the actual software, you're adopting the idea that this is a practice that you ought to be doing in the first place. So, if you're a marketing person, and you adopt some marketing software, you're not just saying, "Okay, now, I can write emails and send them to people." (00:55:24): There's all sorts of process around that. You're organizing stuff into campaigns. You're measuring click-through rates. You're calculating cost of acquisition and all that stuff probably comes equipped with a tool because those are the right practices to do when you're doing this sort of marketing exercise. And whether you knew about it before or you learned it from the tool, like as a buyer for this kind of product, what I'm doing is I'm saying like, "Hey, I'm going to bring in this baseline level of marketing competency into my organization, that this is the worst we can do is whatever the tool defaults are."
turns.zh: 如果你回想一下很多B2B软件是如何诞生的，往往是因为某个大公司的中层人员实施了某个流程，然后他们发现这个流程真的很有效，可能会想，"或许我们应该让它更简单。"于是他们在内部开发一个小工具，同事们就能按按钮，事情就能顺利进行。然后他们把这个流程和工具打包，成立一家初创公司。这整个过程重复了无数次。所以，当你采用这种工具时，你不仅是采用了实际的软件，还接受了这样一个理念：这首先应该是一种你应该实践的做法。比如，如果你是一名营销人员，采用某款营销软件，不只是说"好吧，现在我可以写邮件发给别人了"。（00:55:24）：背后还有各种流程。你要把内容组织成营销活动，衡量点击率，计算获客成本等等，这些功能很可能都和工具捆绑在一起，因为这些都是做营销活动时应该遵循的正确做法。无论你之前是否了解这些，还是从工具中学到的，作为这类产品的买家，我要说的是，我要把这种基准级别的营销能力引入我的组织，至少不能低于工具的默认设置。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. So, you're basically buying into a way of working when you're adopting a piece of software, not just have this problem I need solved.
turns.zh: 有意思。所以，采用一款软件时，本质上你是在接受一种工作方式，而不只是解决一个具体问题。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, exactly, and I think the most salient example of this is if you've ever seen like a company adopt an ERP product, it's the most painful thing you can imagine. It's doing deep surgery. They have to redo all of their internal processes and the way they manage inventory and all this kind of stuff, but they're willing to do it because they know that this is a battle-tested way of making sure that you're actually doing good management of resources. So, they're like, "We're growing up now. It's time for us to adopt these best practices. In order to do that, we have to adopt this tool, and we will conform to whatever the tool is best is to do."
turns.zh: 是的，没错。我认为最典型的例子就是，当你看到一家公司采用ERP产品时，这简直是能想象到的最痛苦的过程。就好比进行深度手术，他们必须重新设计所有内部流程、库存管理方式等等，但他们愿意这么做，因为他们深知这是一种经过实战验证的资源管理方法。所以他们会说：“我们现在要成长了，是时候采用这些最佳实践了。为了实现这一目标，我们必须采用这个工具，并按照工具的最佳使用方式来操作。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This connects to a couple things I know about Linear, one is what you've shared of just avoiding these customizations requests from people. Do you have a very opinionated way of here's how you should operate in order to build a great functioning product, org, and company in general? I'm just connecting threads here.
