One is like we're going to avoid letting people customize too much because we know they'll have a bad time, and then two is just this idea of we are opinionated about the way you should work in Linear, and it's like you have a Linear method, I think it's called, of just like here's how product team should operate based on everything we've seen be successful.
turns.zh: 这让我联想到我对Linear的了解。首先，你提到要避免用户过多定制需求。你们是否有一种非常明确的运营理念，认为必须按照特定方式来构建优秀的运作产品、组织和公司？我只是在把这些线索串联起来。第一点是避免用户过度定制，因为我们知道这会带来糟糕的体验；第二点是Linear团队对最佳实践的坚持，似乎有一套基于成功经验的标准化方法。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. It's definitely connected in a way, and I think sometimes when people talk about... You mentioned like being opinionated, and I think sometimes when people talk about being opinionated, it can feel like they're almost saying like, "Hey, this is arbitrary," like your opinion and my opinion, they're just too opinions, man. Neither is right or wrong. What we try to do is find where there's actual consensus amongst a lot of different high performing teams, and then we can take those practices and say like, "Okay, for a team that isn't already practicing this, can we give them a button so that they can start practicing this?" (00:57:56): When we see companies doing a really good job of managing their triage queue, but it's very manual, we're like, "Okay, can we automate this? And then for this other company that really needs it that they don't know this is what they need, can we just give them a button to activate this?" And now they have the practice within their org, too.
turns.zh: 是的，确实存在关联。有时候当人们谈论“固执己见”时，可能会让人觉得他们在说“嘿，这完全是主观判断”，比如“你的观点和我的观点一样，两者都错”。但我们的做法是寻找在多个高绩效团队中达成共识的实践，然后将这些实践提炼出来，比如“对于尚未采用这种方法的团队，我们能否为他们提供一个按钮，让他们开始实践？”（00:57:56）：当我们看到有些公司能出色管理分诊队列，但方式非常手动时，我们会说：“好吧，我们能否将其自动化？”而对于那些急需某项功能却尚未意识到需求的公司，我们会直接为他们添加一个激活该功能的按钮。现在这些实践在他们的组织内也得到了推广。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, I think the takeaway here is when you choose a tool, recognize it's going to change the way you operate and be thoughtful about is this the way we want to work versus just we just have a problem we want solved?
turns.zh: 所以我认为关键在于选择工具时，要意识到它将改变你的运营方式，并认真思考：这是我们想要的工作方式，还是仅仅为了解决当前问题？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 是的，完全正确。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to something, a thread that's come up a couple of times in our chat is the way you collaborate internally. It feels like there's a pretty unique way. You said you were on all the sales calls. Is there anything that you can share about how you collaborate internally, how the different functions collaborate that may be unlike how other companies operate that might be helpful for them to learn from?
turns.zh: 我想再回归到一个话题——我们聊天中多次提到的内部协作方式。感觉你们的协作方式非常独特。你提到自己参与了所有销售电话。能否分享一下内部协作的具体方式，以及不同职能部门如何协作？这些可能与其他公司的运作方式不同，或许值得他们借鉴。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yes. Something that's worked really, really well for us is we think of product management as partially like a go-to-market discipline in the same way that sales and marketing are, right? When you talk to people and like, "Hey, tell me how product management works in your company," they'll probably say something about like, "Well, there's engineering product and design. They work in this triad, and here's how they interact and collaborate," and we all understand why that's useful, why that's helpful, but this other form of collaboration between product management, sales and marketing, I think it's something that's probably really underexamined and often I feel like in organizations, you actually see some antagonism between product and sales and marketing, and I think that's a shame because when we come together, the way we think about the way that we think about selling is a matter of like... especially because we sell to very expert practitioners, and they have a very sensitive BS detector. (00:59:51): So, a big part of what we try to do is we try to help our marketing team pick exactly the right word and the right phrasing to make us sound native to the language that our customers speak and also-
turns.zh:
是的。对我们非常有效的一个做法是，我们将产品管理视为与销售和市场营销同等重要的市场导入学科，对吧？当你问别人“产品管理在你们公司是如何运作的？”时，他们可能会说：“嗯，产品团队和设计团队合作，形成三角协作，这里是他们如何互动与合作的”，而我们都明白这种协作方式很有用、很有帮助。但产品管理、销售和市场营销之间的另一种协作形式，可能还没有得到充分重视。在很多公司里，你甚至能看到产品与销售、市场营销之间的矛盾，这实在令人遗憾，因为当我们携手合作时，我们对销售的理解会变得更深刻——尤其是因为我们的客户都是行业专家，他们对虚假宣传的警惕性极高。

（00:59:51）：所以，我们的主要工作重点是帮助营销团队准确选择词汇和表达方式，让我们的表述符合客户的语言习惯，同时——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You're talking about engineers is my sense, right?
turns.zh: 你说的是工程师，是吧？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah. Engineers is a big one, but even product managers, right?
turns.zh: 是的。工程师是关键群体，但产品经理同样重要，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Like product managers know when... They know what the job is like. So, when you come in, you say the wrong words, people give you stink eye.
turns.zh: 比如产品经理知道何时该用何种术语。他们清楚这份工作的本质。所以，如果你用词不当，人们会给你脸色看。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Don't call them project managers.
turns.zh: 别把他们叫成项目经理。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, exactly, for example. So, I think that's a big part of what we have to do. So, on our PM team, we actually have a full-time product marketer, and her job is to... Tactically, it's like all the change logs come from her, all the release notes, and also she's always crafting the language for whatever upcoming release that we're building and working directly with the teams and trying to figure out how to talk about it, and then once we go out and build the campaigns, build assets and things like that, that's where a lot of the language is coming from. It's coming from the work that she's doing and then with sales, they're validating all that message in the field. They're saying the words to customers directly and telling you if it's sticking or not, and then you can have a really good feedback cycle between those three disciplines.
turns.zh: 对啊，比如说。所以我认为这正是我们需要努力的重点。在我们的产品管理团队中，我们专门配备了一位全职的产品营销人员，她的工作职责包括：从战术层面处理所有变更日志和发布说明，同时为即将推出的产品版本精心构思宣传语，并与团队直接合作，确定沟通策略。等到我们正式开展推广活动、制作宣传素材等工作时，大部分宣传内容都源自她的工作成果。而销售团队则在实地验证这些信息的有效性，他们直接向客户传递信息，判断信息是否被接受。这样一来，这三个部门就能形成一个良好的反馈循环。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What I've seen you refer to this way of working as is a double triangle, which is I think a complement to the PM, engineer, designer. Talk about that and give us a visual of what that looks like.
turns.zh: 我注意到你将这种工作方式称为双三角模型，我认为这是产品经理、工程师和设计师三角协作的补充。能否谈谈这个模型，并给我们展示一下它的视觉图示？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, I think PMs, like product managers, we often have a tough time trying to explain like, "What is your job?" It's a little bit of everything. I think the job that I do that we see it as is you're taking the building side of the organization and the selling side of the organization and bringing it together. You're taking all of the commercial motivations and goals of the company and making sure that what you build actually solves for those goals, and you're tempering that with what's possible and where the opportunities are to actually build stuff. So, to me, it's the PM in the middle, and then you have engineering, product design, and then sales, marketing, product management on the other side.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得产品经理（PM）和产品总监（PM）这类职位，在解释“你的工作职责是什么”时往往会遇到难题。我们的工作职责涵盖方方面面。我认为，我所从事的工作本质上是将企业的研发部门和销售部门紧密结合起来，把握公司的商业动机和目标，确保所开发的产品能够真正实现这些目标，同时还要兼顾技术可行性和市场机遇。因此，在我看来，产品经理始终处于两者之间的桥梁位置——一端是工程、产品设计等技术团队，另一端是销售、市场等商业团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: PM is always in the middle-
turns.zh: 产品经理始终处于中间位置——

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Indeed.
turns.zh: 确实如此。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... but I think that's true from the perspective of PM, and I love this visual of just the PM is connecting the builders to the sellers, and you're involved in both worlds. This connects very directly to Brian Chesky's whole thing about how PMs should be doing marketing. So, the way they changed it, every PM is also PMM, and there's no more... They're product marketers now. That's their title and that's like the extreme version of what you're describing.
turns.zh: 嗯……但从产品经理的角度来看，我觉得这确实如此。我特别喜欢这种产品经理连接开发者和销售者的视觉效果，而你同时身处这两个领域。这与布莱恩·切斯基关于产品经理应该参与市场营销的观点紧密相连。现在他们把每个产品经理都改称为PMM，不再有其他头衔……他们现在就是产品营销人员了。这就是你的工作描述的极端版本。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, and I think Apple's been doing that way for forever, too.
turns.zh: 是的。是的，我觉得苹果公司也一直这么做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So, the advice here is if you're a PM at a B2B business, lean into the sales and marketing side of it, lean into the go-to-market.
turns.zh: 明白了。所以给B2B企业的产品经理的建议是，深入销售和营销领域，深入市场推广。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, and in fact, if you're leaving something on the table in terms of the kind of impact that you are having at your job, that's probably the thing that you're leaving on the table. You're probably already doing a good job of collaborating with engineering and design. It's probably the sort of sell side that there's an opportunity for you to have more impact.
turns.zh: 是的。事实上，如果你在工作中没有充分发挥影响力，那可能就是你忽视的部分。你可能已经在与工程和设计团队合作得很好。真正有更多影响力的机会可能在销售端。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to make it even more concrete for PMs that are like, "Okay, I want to do this. I want to do what Linear's doing. I'm going to get more salesy." What does it look like when someone is more is in this double triangle working more closely with sales? You talked about being on sales calls. What else there can you share of just like, "Here, try these things"?
turns.zh: 为了让那些想效仿Linear的产品经理更具体地理解，我举个例子：当有人更紧密地与销售团队合作时，具体会是什么样子？你提到了参与销售电话会议。还有其他可以分享的建议吗？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: I think originate the message that you send to your audience. There's a lot of things that marketing does, which you are never going to necessarily touch. There's always demand gen and figuring out channel strategy and all this kind of stuff, like sure. That's a peer marketing concern, but actually picking the words and where the emphasis is, like you should understand the customer at a pretty deep level, probably deeper than any other group at the company because of the kinds of requirements gathering, discovery that you're doing. So, you're going to know the native language that your customers speak a lot better and help your marketing team originate those words.
turns.zh: 我认为关键在于为你的受众传递核心信息。营销部门有很多工作，你不一定需要参与。比如需求生成、渠道策略制定等等，这些都是营销团队的职责。但真正需要你关注的是如何构思信息、确定重点。比如你应该对客户有深刻的理解，可能比公司其他部门更深入，因为你参与了需求收集和探索阶段。因此，你能更准确地掌握客户的语言习惯，帮助营销团队构思合适的表达。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So, basically be really involved in the product marketing, the writing, the emails, the headlines, the website?
turns.zh: 明白了。所以基本上要深度参与产品营销，包括文案撰写、邮件设计、标题优化、网站建设等？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, yeah, exactly. I know the word product marketing is also so overloaded. They do so many different things, but it's that sort of content creation piece that you really have an opportunity to contributes to.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。我知道“产品营销”这个词被过度使用了。它涵盖太多内容，但真正能发挥作用的是内容创作部分。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I love how concrete that is. It's like don't think about this concept, product marketing. Just think about the words that your potential customers and customers see. Okay, final area I want to spend a lot of time on is totally different. It's around getting a job.
turns.zh: 是的，我很欣赏这种具体的思路。不要空谈产品营销，而是关注潜在客户和现有客户看到的文字。好的，最后我想重点讨论一个完全不同的话题——找工作。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Oh, yeah. Okay.
turns.zh: 哦，是的。好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You have a pretty unique approach to finding a gig. I heard from the founder of Mode about the very unique way you approached getting a job there. I imagine Linear is a similar boat. What advice can you share with folks that are looking for a job, maybe struggling, that work for you when you were looking for your next gig?
turns.zh: 你找工作的方法很独特。我听说Mode公司的创始人提到你找工作时采用的非传统方式。我猜Linear公司的情况也类似。你能给正在找工作、可能遇到困难的人一些建议吗？这些方法在你自己找工作时也奏效过吗？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Project management is a unique role. Because we do just about everything, you don't really get pigeonholed into being compared along a single dimension with everyone else, and everyone who's hiring PMs, just like when they're hiring execs, they're hoping that they bring them on to solve some burning problem that they have. So, it's your job when you're in the interview process to figure out what that burning problem is. So, put on your discovery hat and go figure out what is the actual job to be done of the hiring manager when they're bringing on a new PM onto their team? And if you can do that and then make a good case that you are the person to solve that problem, then hiring you becomes a binary choice between do I hire the solution to my problem or do I hire someone else? (01:05:48): And I think what ends up happening a lot is when you're in a interview process, you're just trying to put your best foot forward, trying to say that you're great at everything. You have very few weaknesses. Maybe you tried too hard, like whatever, but everyone's going to say that. So, you're just one of end people, and you want to make yourself a little bit of just you versus the field. You're the solution to a problem and then everyone else is like a roll of the dice.
turns.zh:
项目管理是一个独特的角色。由于我们几乎要做所有事情，你不会被局限于与其他人进行单一维度的比较。招聘项目经理的公司，就像招聘高管一样，都希望他们能解决手头亟待解决的问题。因此，在面试过程中，关键在于你要弄清楚对方的核心需求。换句话说，你要戴上侦探帽，深入挖掘招聘经理在引入新项目经理时真正面临的痛点。如果你能成功证明自己是解决这些问题的理想人选，那么招聘你就成了一个非此即彼的二选一决策——要么你能解决问题，要么另觅他人。

（01:05:48）：我发现很多面试者都只是想展现自己最好的一面，总说自己无所不能、几乎没有弱点。或许他们确实努力过，但这种说辞太常见了。所以你只是千篇一律的普通人，而你需要突出自己的独特价值，证明自己是解决问题的高手，而其他候选人只是碰运气。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, the way you're describing it is the company has a job to be done, say it's drive growth of some feature. In this case, it's like for Linear, just build a killer or successful B2B product. I don't know. That's a broad one. Usually, you're not interviewing for head of product role, so that's maybe too broad. So, it's like what is this PM role's job to be done at the company and then help convince them you are the best person to do that job and solve this problem for them.
turns.zh: 你所描述的场景是，公司有特定的需求，比如推动某个功能的增长。以 Linear 为例，可能需要打造一款成功的 B2B 产品。我不知道这是否太宽泛了。通常你面试的不是产品总监级别职位，所以这个定义可能太模糊了。关键在于明确项目经理在公司中的具体职责，并说服对方你就是解决这些问题的理想人选。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, and a lot of times when you take that approach, it'll feel like you already work there, and the way that I did this, like I got advice from a friend. He said like, "I was interviewing for this job at Mode that you referenced." I'm like, "How should I approach it?" He's like, "Just act like you already worked there. What would you do?" And then it's like, "Okay, I could do that." So, then when you're in this interview process and someone's asking you questions. He goes, "Do you have any questions for me?" You can ask them like, "What are your OKRs this quarter? How can someone help you achieve those?" You can be that specific about it, and they're like, "Oh, yeah, sure. I can tell you about the exact thing that I'm doing this quarter, and then you'll have some level of intelligence about what people are actually trying to solve because I think often we just get stuck in these very high level general types of questions like, "What's the company goals sand all that kind of stuff, and it's like, no, you can get really specific. If you were collaborating with that person in your job, what would you say to them?
turns.zh: 是的，采用这种方法时，你会感觉自己已经在那里工作了。我曾从朋友那里获得建议。他说：“我在 Mode 面试时，你提到的那个职位。”我问：“该怎么应对？”他说：“就当你已经在那里工作了。你会怎么做？”然后我说：“好吧，我可以做到。”在面试过程中，当对方问：“你有什么问题吗？”你可以反问：“你本季度的 OKR 目标是什么？如何帮助你达成这些目标？”这样既具体又实用。而对方可能会说：“哦，好的，我可以告诉你本季度具体的工作内容。”这样你就能真正了解他们正在解决的问题，因为我们常被困在诸如“公司目标是什么”之类的高大上问题中，而实际上，深入了解对方的具体需求才最重要。比如，如果你在工作中与这个人合作，你会对他们说什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how actionable this advice is. There's obviously an element of this takes work and time. A lot of people are interviewing at a lot of companies, trying to find a job, is part of your advice. Pick the ones you're most excited about and invest a lot of time in this way of interviewing.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏这种切实可行的建议。当然，这需要投入时间和精力。很多人在多家公司面试，寻找工作机会，这是你建议的一部分。选择最令你兴奋的公司，并投入大量时间进行这种类型的面试。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: You can invest a lot in the ones where you know that you're going to be able to over deliver on. If you understand what they're actually trying to solve, then you know where you're going to have both the highest chance of success of getting hired, but also doing a really great job on the other end of it.
turns.zh: 针对那些你确信自己能超额完成任务的项目，你可以投入大量精力。如果你真正理解他们试图解决的问题，那么你不仅更有可能成功获得录用，还能在后续工作中表现出色。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you talk about how you're like pretending you have the job, pretending you actually have this job as part of the interview process. Oftentimes, as an outsider, you don't have enough information to have a really good thought on what the solution is, and maybe part of it is going to be so wrong because you're like, "I don't actually know. I don't have the data." Do you actually try to reach out to the engineers and designers on the team to try to understand things? How far do you go to try to solve these problems and show them what you can do?
turns.zh: 你提到在面试过程中要假装自己已经获得了这份工作，假装自己正在为这份工作努力。通常，作为局外人，你没有足够的信息来准确理解解决方案，可能部分想法会偏离正轨，因为你会想：“我其实并不知道具体情况，我没有相关数据。”你是否会主动联系团队中的工程师和设计师，试图理解问题所在？你会采取哪些措施来解决这些问题并向他们展示自己的能力？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, you're in the interview loop. These are people that you're going to be working closely with. So, start there. Do your discovery questions, and if there's an area that you think you want to dig, you can ask. There's no harm asking, "Hey, can you put me in touch with an engineering manager who's working on the same problem?" And if no one else is asking, again, you're going to have an extra piece of feedback from that eng manager. So, yeah, like this guy asks really good questions, and it seems like they're really with it. No one else is going to have that piece of feedback. So, during the debrief process.
turns.zh: 是的，你正处于面试环节。这些人将是你的紧密合作伙伴。所以从这里入手。做好探索性提问，如果有某个领域你想深入探讨，可以提出疑问。比如，“能否帮我联系正在处理相同问题的工程经理？”如果其他人没有提出同样的问题，那么你就能从这位工程经理那里获得额外的反馈。所以，如果有人问出这样的问题，说明他对问题思考得很深入，而其他人可能得不到这样的反馈。在汇报环节时，这会成为加分项。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And just asking that question alone will show them how deeply you're thinking about this already?
turns.zh: 仅仅提出这个问题就能让他们看到你对问题的深度思考了吗？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Nan, is there anything else that we have not covered that you want to touch on or share or you think might be helpful to listeners before we get to a very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 太棒了。南，还有没有我们没有涉及到，但你想分享给听众，或者认为对他们有帮助的内容呢？在我们进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: I have a very specific point of view on deadlines. I don't know if that's [inaudible 01:09:34] you care.
turns.zh: 我对截止日期有一些独特的看法。我不知道你是否感兴趣。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do it. Fire away.
turns.zh: 那就开始吧。畅所欲言吧。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: I think what often happens is people get depressed about deadlines. It's like, "Hey, here's the ship date," and then you never make it. I don't know if you've had this feeling before.
turns.zh: 我觉得很多人对截止日期感到沮丧。比如，“嘿，截止日期到了，”但你永远也赶不上。不知道你有没有过这种感受。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely, with some deadlines.
turns.zh: 是的，我在一些截止日期上确实有过这种情况。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: You were an engineer before too, right? So, it's just like engineers is basically like, "Oh, yeah. Yeah, deadlines, they're complete fabrications," and the only way to make deadlines real is to take them so seriously that they are basically like a P0 problem, and everything else has to not matter in comparison to the deadline because that's the only way you're going to be able to signal to the team and also to all the stakeholders that you're actually taking it seriously. So, my feeling on deadlines is don't have too many of them, and when you do, it's a P0. So, the engineer is working on it. They don't get to work on anything else. (01:10:28): It's like, "Oh, I need them for this," like nope. Nope. You're not pulling them off of anything. We're doing this. As a PM, your job is to just cut as much scope as possible to make it possible to hit that deadline. Like what are the things actually blocking us from doing it? Because what you want to do is at the moment where you have to make the go, no-go call on whether to ship, you want to be able to actually have a product that you can say yes to. It might not have all the features you had wanted or whatever, and you can say no. You can make that choice, but you want to set yourself up to be in a position where you can actually say yes or no to something, because what often happens is like we want this thing. Well, it's not even close to being done yet, so there's no possible way we can say yes. I can't ship it. It's half broken. It's like, "No, no, no. You want to get to a point where it works. It might not be the product that you want, but it is an actual real product that you can conceivably ship."
turns.zh: 你以前也是工程师，对吧？所以，工程师们通常会想：“哦，是啊，这些截止日期都是虚构出来的”，而要让截止日期真正成为现实的唯一方法，就是把它们视为头等大事，这样一来其他事情都得让步，因为只有这样你才能向团队和所有利益相关者表明你真的很重视它。所以我对截止日期的看法是，别设太多截止日期，而一旦设定了，就必须把它当作头等大事。（01:10:28）就像，“哦，我需要它们来做这个”，别这样。别这样。你不能把其他任务从日程中抽走。我们要专注于手头的任务。作为产品经理，你的职责就是尽可能削减项目范围，确保能在截止日期前达成目标。比如，阻碍我们实现目标的因素是什么？因为当你必须决定是否上线产品时，你希望能拿出一个可以肯定会成功的产品。它可能没有你期望的所有功能，但至少是一个可以上线的产品。你可以说不，但你得确保自己有能力做出选择，因为很多时候我们会想：“嗯，这东西还没完成呢，现在怎么可能上线呢？”这太不现实了。我不能把它上线，它还半成品呢。这时候你得说：“不，不，不。你得先让它能正常运行。即使它不是你理想中的产品，但至少得是个能上线的真实产品。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, you said that don't have too many deadlines, but when you do, make sure you... Everyone understands these are actual deadlines. When do you decide it's worth having a deadline? Is it like a marketing launch sort of thing? What's worthy of a deadline in your experience?
turns.zh: 所以你说别设太多截止日期，但一旦设定了，就得确保所有人都明白这些是真正的截止日期。什么时候你会觉得值得设定一个截止日期呢？是像市场推广活动之类的吗？在你看来，什么样的事情值得设定截止日期？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, it's usually having to do with some kind of external marketing type of exercise that you're try to hit.
turns.zh: 是的，通常和一些外部营销活动有关，比如你要赶在某个时间点上线。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it.
turns.zh: 明白了。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: And I think that that's the other thing that I think. As builders, we can often look at launch dates and stuff like that. It's like, "Oh, who cares if it's a little bit later or we skip this change log," or whatever it is, and I think that that's really a... I don't know. It makes me go crazy when I hear people say that in all honesty. With marketing and communication with customers, you basically have a limited amount of opportunities to do so. A year is 365 days. There are 12 months. Each of those months has about four weeks. There's some rhythm where you get to have 50-ish weeks to say something to your audience once a week, or you get to have 12 months to say something really big or four quarters to say something huge. If you miss one of those opportunities, you don't get it back again. You can't time travel back and say like, "Okay, actually, let's redo first quarter and say this message that we wish we could have gotten into the field."
turns.zh: 我觉得还有一点。作为开发者，我们经常会关注发布日期之类的事情。比如，“哦，晚几天又有什么关系呢？或者跳过这个变更日志又怎样？”之类的，我觉得这真的很……说实话，每次听到有人这么说我都抓狂。特别是涉及市场和客户沟通的时候，你能利用的机会其实很有限。一年有365天，12个月，每个月大约四周。时间有它的规律性，你每年有大约50周的时间，每周向受众传递一次信息，或者每年有12个月的时间来发布重大消息，或者分成四个季度来做大动作。如果错过其中一个机会，就再也无法挽回了。你没法回到过去说，“好吧，我们重新规划第一季度，再次传递那个我们本想在现场发布的信息。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is such a powerful point. I could see the sales marketing, go-to-market element of your job coming out there. I imagine everyone that's in that field's like, "Yes, this is exactly right." Maybe just the last question along this line. So, I love this idea of taking deadlines very seriously when you commit to a deadline. At the same time, as you pointed out, it creates a lot of stress knowing there's a deadline we have to hit. So, one lever you've mentioned is cutting scope. Another is just people spending more time estimating to have more accurate deadlines. You invest in that. How do you think about just for an engineering team to come into a deadline, how much to spend on de-risking and estimating versus just, "Let's just do our best and then we'll cut and adjust"?
turns.zh: 这真是太棒了。我能感受到你所从事的工作中销售和市场推广的元素。这让我觉得，所有从事这一领域的人都会感叹：“没错，完全正确！” 或许最后一个问题可以沿着这个思路继续下去。我喜欢你提到的这种严肃对待截止日期的做法。同时，正如你所指出的，知道必须在截止日期前完成任务会带来巨大压力。你提到的两种应对策略，一是缩减项目范围，二是让团队花更多时间进行估算以确保更准确的截止日期。你对此进行了投入。那么对于一个工程团队来说，面对截止日期时，如何平衡投入资源用于规避风险和估算成本与直接全力以赴然后再进行调整呢？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: This might be my hot take, but we do almost no estimating in order to hit deadlines. What we do is we ship as early as we can. The thing we talked about earlier where if by the time that 10% of the time has elapsed, you have a working thing, you can now spend the rest of the time deciding whether or not you want to do another iteration or you want to polish that thing and get it to be a shippable state. So, you're setting up your future self to be able to make that decision. So, none of this is... You can't go into this at the very last moment and say like, "Okay, now, we have to take the deadline seriously." You have to do it from the beginning and commit to the process of going very fast, iterating early, and then putting yourself in a position where you can say yes or no to a product.
turns.zh: 这或许是我个人的看法，但我们几乎不进行估算来赶截止日期。我们所做的是尽早交付产品。正如我们之前讨论的，如果在项目进行到10%的时间点时，你已经有了一个可用的产品原型，那么剩余的时间就可以用来决定是继续迭代还是将产品打磨至可交付状态。这样你就能为未来的自己铺路，让他们能够做出明智的决策。而不是在最后一刻才说“好吧，现在我们必须认真对待截止日期了”。你必须从一开始就投入精力，坚持快速迭代、尽早交付的流程，最终才能在产品决策上游刃有余。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So interesting and so different from the way most companies operate. Nan, this was everything I was hoping it'd be. I think this is going to help a lot of people build much better product, which would be good for the world if more products are like Linear. With that, we reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 太有趣了，和大多数公司的运作方式截然不同。南，这正是我们所期待的。我相信这将帮助许多人打造出更优质的产品，如果有更多产品能像Linear这样，那对整个世界来说都是好事。现在，我们来进行激动人心的闪电问答环节。你们准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, let's do it.
turns.zh: 好的，开始吧。第一个问题：你向别人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, let's do it. Okay, first question. What are two or three books that you have recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 我推荐最多的书是唐·诺曼的《日常事物的设计》。我最初是在大学上人机交互课时读到这本书的，在我读过的所有书中，这本书让我从产品设计的视角看待身边的一切事物。无论是使用的铅笔，还是打开的门，都像是经过设计的产品。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: I think the one book that I recommend the most is The Design of Everyday Things by Don Norman. I read it originally in college for an HCI class I was taking, and I think of everything I've ever read, it's the thing that caused me to see the world from the perspective of everything you interact with as a product. Every pencil that you use, every door that you open is a product that somebody designed.
turns.zh: 这是这本书的主要启示吗？因为它被提及很多次，而且已经出版很久了。所以对于没读过或没时间读的人来说，这就是你最重要的收获。一切都是有人设计的，而且总有改进的空间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And is that the big takeaway from that book? Because it comes up a lot, and it's such an old book. So, I guess for someone that hasn't read or maybe doesn't have time to read, it is the big takeaway for you. Someone designed everything and there's a reason things aren't great, and they can be improved.
turns.zh: 是的。前几天我就有这样的体会。我在附近的咖啡馆，看到一个孩子把门把手扯下来了。那是咖啡馆的门。门是推拉式的，但把手设计得像可以拉开一样。这就是书中提到的典型例子，设计中的谜团。是啊。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I saw this the other day. I was at a café in my neighborhood, and I saw a kid rip a handle off a door, like of the café. He pulled it so hard, it came right off because it was a push door, but it had a handle that looked like you could pull it, and that's one of the canonical examples of the book because [inaudible 01:15:25] are just mysteries. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。前几天我也遇到过类似的情况。我在附近的咖啡馆，看到一个孩子把门把手扯下来了。那是咖啡馆的门。门是推拉式的，但把手设计得像可以拉开一样。这就是书中提到的典型例子，设计中的谜团。是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Next question. Do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show you've really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 太棒了。下一个问题。你最近有没有看过特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: I watched The Diplomat on Netflix. I think it was terrific. It's really fun, easy watch. It has some West Wing vibes if you were into that back in the day.
turns.zh: 我在Netflix上看了《外交官》。我觉得这部剧很棒。看得很轻松愉快。它有点《白宫风云》的风格，要是你当年看过那部剧的话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, have you seen the second season?
turns.zh: 对啊，你看过第二季吗？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, I finished the second season. Yeah.
turns.zh: 看过了，第二季我已经看完了。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I wasn't as excited about the second season, just to put that out there. The first season was really good and then just went off a little like, "Okay. I guess it's cool," but stuff like that.
turns.zh: 不过我对第二季没那么兴奋，跟你说实话。第一季确实很棒，但第二季有点偏离了轨道，就感觉“嗯，还行吧”之类的。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, it got a little like spy thrillery, I think.
turns.zh: 是啊，它变得有点像间谍惊悚片的感觉了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, cool, but still really good and on Netflix. Okay, cool. Do you have a favorite product you recently discovered that you really like?
turns.zh: 好的，挺酷的，但还是很不错的，而且在Netflix上能看。好的，不错。你最近有没有发现什么特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: I didn't discover it, but I discovered a version of it that was really interesting. There's a pen. Actually, I have one on my desk. It's called the Sakura Micron. I don't know if you use these. It's like a felt tip pen. It's really great. It was originally invented in Japan for artists to draw comic books and stuff, and you can use it for anything. I use it for journaling or whatever, but I was on Amazon. I was trying to buy more, and I found a package that said like, "Bible Study Kit." I was like, "Why is this labeled Bible Study Kit?" And it was literally just the pen in four different colors, and it was because the thing doesn't bleed through pages. So, if you have a Bible, which they often have these really flimsy newsprint pages. It's not going to bleed through. (01:16:51): And it's just really interesting to me that someone marketed a normal package of these pens as a Bible study kit and for people who were looking for that keyword, and it was official, too. It was not something hacked together. It was actually an official packaging of this.
turns.zh: 我倒是没发现新产品，但发现了一个很有趣的版本。有一支笔。实际上，我桌上就有一支，叫“三文鱼Micron”。不知道你用过没。这是一支毡尖笔，真的很棒。它最初是日本为漫画家设计的，但现在用途很广。我用它写日记之类的，不过我在亚马逊上买的时候发现了一个标着“圣经学习套装”的包裹。我就想，“为什么标圣经学习套装啊？”结果里面就是四种颜色的Micron笔，因为它不会渗墨。假如你有圣经，里面通常用那种很薄的纸质页面，用这种笔就不会渗了。（01:16:51）这让我觉得很有趣，有人把这种普通笔套装包装成圣经学习套装，专门针对搜索这个关键词的人，而且还是官方包装，不是什么山寨货。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. What a unique pen choice. Two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to and find useful in work or in life?
turns.zh: 太棒了。真是个独特的笔选。再问两个问题。你有没有一个生活格言，经常回想，觉得在工作或生活中很有用？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: The correct amount is too much minus one, and I think this ties into the try the extreme version of it of a thing where... I don't know, like a stupid example, like how much pizza do you want to eat? It's like, well, five slices was too many. I feel bad. Then four was probably the right number, and then if you want to find the right number, sometimes you just have to really shoot for the edge and then find out what's too much, and then you'll find out exactly what the right amount is.
turns.zh: 正确的数量是太多减一，我觉得这和极端尝试相关。比如，你想吃多少披萨？五片太多，我感觉糟糕。四片可能合适。要想找到合适的数量，有时就得先极端一把，再调整。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love how tactical that is, makes me think about Elon Musk's thing about cutting things. Like one of his formulas for just getting stuff done, one of them is just cut stuff before trying to optimize it and automate it, and his advice is if you don't bring back 10% of things, you cut, you're not cutting enough.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种策略性思维，让我想起埃隆·马斯克关于砍掉东西的理念。他说要先砍掉再优化自动化，其中一个建议是先砍掉10%的东西，再调整。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对啊，就是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. You worked at Everlane for a number of years, and you shared the rough idea of a story around a shirt, maybe a bestseller that they have now, and how you helped create a bestselling women's shirt. Can you share that story?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。你在Everlane工作了好几年，你分享过一个关于某款畅销女式衬衫的故事，讲你如何帮助打造这款畅销品。能分享一下这个故事吗？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah. So, I mean, to be clear, I witnessed the creation. I don't think I had a direct hand in it, but yeah. So, I saw this advertisement the other day on Instagram for... It's called the Women's Box-Cut Tee, and it's a wide and short for women, and I looked, and it had 20 colors of it, and it sells super well, and I remember when we created this thing, and it was because there was a batch of defective men's t-shirts. They all came in an inch and a half too short. So, we couldn't sell them. You would have your belly button sticking out. No one wants to wear of that. So, what we did was like, well, we have to salvage the inventory because we were a very small company, and we had to make cash flow, and we couldn't just damage it out. (01:19:06): So, the design team and the marketing team came together, and they said, "Okay. Here's what we're going to do. We're going to cut another two inches off of this and make it really cropped and market it towards women as like a cropped boxed-tee silhouette, and we did that. We're like, "Okay, hopefully, we can salvage this inventory and not have to take a write-down." It sold out in a week, and we're like, "Oh, okay. I guess we just made a hit product," and it's one of these things where it's very hard to know what this was. Was this a marketing thing? Was this a design thing? I don't know, but you just come together, and you find the right product market fit in the weirdest way.
turns.zh: 是的。所以，我想说清楚一点，我亲眼见证了这个产品的诞生。我不认为自己直接参与了其中，但确实如此。前几天我在Instagram上看到一则广告，叫做“女式短款剪裁T恤”，专为女性设计，款式宽松短款。我看了一下，共有20种颜色，而且销量非常好。记得我们开发这款产品时，是因为有一批男式T恤有缺陷，全部短了1.5英寸，根本卖不出去。那样穿的话，肚脐会露出来，没人会想穿这种衣服。于是我们灵机一动，决定把多余库存利用起来，毕竟我们当时还是一家小公司，急需现金流，不能让库存积压。（01:19:06）于是设计团队和营销团队集思广益，决定把这批T恤再剪短两英寸，打造出短款女式剪裁T恤，并以短款设计作为卖点推广。最终产品大获成功，一周内售罄。我们当时就感叹：“哇，原来我们打造了一款爆款产品。”这个案例很难归类——到底是营销成功，还是设计出色？我也说不清，但关键是各部门通力合作，奇迹般地找到了合适的市场定位。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that it's still going.
turns.zh: 这产品现在还很火。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, it's still going. Originally, it was just white. Now, there's like 20 colors.
turns.zh: 是啊，一直很火。最初只有白色款，现在有20种颜色了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man. I love how many industries you have worked in: fashion, data analytics, project management. I don't know what's next. There's more, I imagine. Nan, this was incredible. I really appreciate making time for this. Like I said, I think we're going to have helped a lot of people build better products. Two final questions, where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and learn more? And how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: 天哪。你涉足的行业真多：时尚、数据分析、项目管理。我都不知道接下来会做什么了。应该还有更多领域吧。南，这次交流太棒了。感谢你抽出时间。正如我之前所说，我相信我们能帮助很多人打造更好的产品。最后两个问题：如果听众想了解更多信息，哪里可以找到你？他们又该如何为你提供有用的反馈？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, I'm on X/Twitter as the thenanyu. It's T-H-E and then my name, and if they have any feedback about Linear, we're very happy to take it, especially for people who use it in their day-to-day. We really want to hear from users.
turns.zh: 是的，我在X/Twitter上的账号是thenanyu。用户名是T-H-E再加我的名字。如果大家对Linear有任何反馈，我们非常乐意倾听，尤其是那些日常使用它的人的意见。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the best way for them to share that? Is it tweet at you? Is it go to the website? What do you recommend?
turns.zh: 他们分享反馈的最佳方式是什么？是发推文吗？还是访问网站？你建议哪种方式？

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Oh, yeah. You can tweet at us. You can DM me on Twitter. My DMs are open, so it's all good.
turns.zh: 哦，对。可以发推文给我。也可以在Twitter上私信我。我的私信功能一直开着，所以都可以。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Nan, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。南，非常感谢你今天的分享。

turns.speaker: Nan Yu
turns.en: Yeah, of course. Thanks, Lenny.
turns.zh: 是的，当然。谢谢你，莱尼。
